title: Dolly Parton Believed Wine Was for Everyone—Not Just Experts
summary:
The Grammy-winning country artist and humanitarian, who launched her first line of wines in 2024, believed in wine as a catalyst for togetherness.

The post Dolly Parton Believed Wine Was for Everyone—Not Just Experts appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Metaphorically speaking, Dolly Parton turned water into wine. 

The 11-time Grammy-winning country artist and songwriter, who died on Tuesday, August 25, after a brief illness, performed miracles everywhere her peep toe heels and rhinestone-embellished cowboy boots took her. 

Listing her humanitarian efforts would take longer than her discography, but we would be remiss not to mention The Dollywood Foundation, which provides annual scholarships to high school seniors in Sevier County, Tennessee, or its Imagination Library program, which has gifted over 330 million books to children across five countries since 1995. (The Library of Congress even deemed Parton a “titan of children’s literacy.”) 

Parton personally donated $1 million to Hurricane Helene recovery efforts in 2024, which was then matched by her East Tennessee businesses. She also notably donated $1 million to Tennessee’s Vanderbilt University’s coronavirus vaccine research in April 2020, which led to the development of the Moderna Covid vaccine. 

This hardly scratches the surface of the cultural icon’s philanthropic efforts, as her metaphorical wine was ever-flowing from her generous heart. But Parton also turned grapes into wine. 

In July 2024, the “Jolene” singer launched her first line of wines, Dolly Wines, in collaboration with Parton Family Cellars and wine giant Accolade Wines (renamed Vinarchy after its 2025 merger with Pernod Ricard Winemakers). Described as “easy-drinking, light-hearted and vibrant,” Dolly Wines offers a Pinot Noir and a Chardonnay in the U.S. (U.K. wine lovers are offered a Prosecco and a rosé), the latter earning an impressive 93 points from Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large Tonya Pitts. 

Pitts praised the wine’s white peach, melon, and blood orange aromas, as well as flavors of Golden Delicious apple, grapefruit, ginger, and green tea—though Parton may not have been able to detect such precise notes herself, as an admitted wine novice. Her unconventional contribution to the wine industry is part of what makes it so charming—and accessible.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Wine Enthusiast (@wineenthusiast)

Dolly Parton’s Relationship With Wine Embodied Togetherness, Not Snobbery

Despite writing lyrics like “And do you all recall the time we all got drunk on homemade wine? That was in the better part of life we’ve left behind,” Parton wasn’t exactly a wine connoisseur. 

“I always like to test everything that I’m involved with, and they do bring the wine for me to taste. But I try to leave those kinds of things to the experts,” Parton said in a 2024 Wine Spectator interview when asked about her level of involvement. “I wouldn’t know the first thing about how to make a good wine or be able to say for certain if it’s this or that,” she continued, making it crystal clear she was neither an authority in viniculture nor did she wish to be the next serious celebrity winemaker, akin to someone like the late Sam Neill. 

Like many aspects of Parton’s life and career, her foray into the wine business was about people. “My wine is for the regular people out there who like to have a good time, people who love together, who get together with friends and family,” she explained, noting that “it isn’t necessarily for somebody so highfalutin who knows this and that and has a bottle that’s 200 years old.” 

Of course, Parton clarified that there’s no harm in hoping collectors try her wine, but she created a line of palatable, affordable bottles with the everyman in mind. 

It’s not outlandish to say ordering a glass at a winery, restaurant, or wine bar can be daunting for a casual wine drinker, who may not have “tannin” or “tertiary aroma” in their vocabulary.

According to a 2018 study, 30% of Americans are frustrated by lengthy wine menus and 19% are intimidated by sommeliers. Similarly, 2022 research found that three in four people are intimidated by the “rules of wine.” Considering Parton insisted her brand is for “anybody who likes to drink wine,” Dolly Wines repels these kinds of stats.  

This dedication to the notion that wine is for everyone is reiterated on the Dolly Wines site, which states that the brand “[draws] from her legendary career in music and her unwavering spirit of inclusivity.”

Dolly Parton’s Appalachian Mountain Childhood Saw Homemade Wine and Moonshine

Parton’s kinship with wine was simultaneously lax and deep-rooted, as her first memories of wine go back to her childhood in Locust Ridge, Tennessee, right outside of Sevierville. One of 12 kids, she grew up in a one-bedroom cabin (which lacked electricity and running water) in the Great Smoky Mountains, the perfect environment for her family’s homemade wine and moonshine.

Made by distilling corn mash in the Smokies, her father’s special moonshine was a sore subject in the Parton household, as her rigid Christian mother didn’t approve of it, despite it helping pay the bills. Appearing on her seventh studio album, Joshua, her song “Daddy’s Moonshine Still” touches on this, as does her 2020 book Dolly Parton, Songteller: My Life in Lyrics.

“He didn’t really want to do it, but people make moonshine in the mountains because they need the income. So Daddy did that for a time, and so did a lot of my relatives,” she wrote of her farmer father.

Illegal during the Prohibition era, making wine and moonshine is deeply ingrained in Appalachian history as an economic necessity, supported by higher altitudes, well-draining soil, and isolation. 

Regarding wine specifically, farmers started growing grapes in the region circa the 18th and 19th centuries, as per Tennessee Homemade Wines. Parton even mentions “all them possum grapes and muscadines” in her 1973 tune “The Better Part of Life.”

Parton was quite candid about not being much of a drinker herself, as she viewed wine as a catalyst for beautiful memories more than anything. Still, her family’s Appalachian survivalist ties to alcoholic beverage production and her warm honesty about a lack of formal wine education made her an unlikely celebrity wine icon for the people. 

As for what will happen to Dolly Wines now that Dolly is gone, it’s hard to say, but considering Sam Neill’s Two Paddocks wine sales boomed directly following his death earlier this summer (Liquorland New Zealand reported a 1,828% increase in brand sales within just a few days of the news), posthumous consumer interest is promising. 

To pour one out for Dolly Parton is to pour one out for an American treasure, and it may as well be from a bottle adorned with butterflies.

title: Provenance 101: What to Know About the Fight Against Wine Counterfeits
summary:
With AI reaching total ubiquity, the issue of verifying provenance has become more prominent than ever before. Here’s how it's evolving.

The post Provenance 101: What to Know About the Fight Against Wine Counterfeits appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Rising AI fakes and high-profile counterfeits make verifiable provenance essential for protecting fine wine authenticity and financial value.
  • Detailed paperwork and physical bottle inspections ensure quality control.
  • Emerging tools like blockchain and digital sensors offer tracking solutions, but high implementation costs and practical limits hinder adoption.

We are living in the era of deepfake, synthetic media. Online, everyone from A-list celebrities to private citizens are posting augmented or entirely fictional photos of themselves using generative AI—innocuous to some, harmful to others, misleading to all. Then there’s the criminal aspect: The FBI estimates that $5 billion has been lost to scammers generating text, images, audio, or videos to trick victims. 

The pressing problem of deepfakes is especially challenging for businesses where value is intrinsically tied to authenticity. Take the wine industry. The 2016 Netflix documentary Sour Grapes tells the story of how Rudy “Dr. Conti” Kurniawan conned collectors out of millions by selling them counterfeit bottles of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, Pétrus, and other highly sought-after wines. Now a decade after the film’s release, with AI reaching total ubiquity, the issue of verifying provenance has become more prominent than ever before.

The Price Tag of Provenance

Provenance is the documented history or the literal paper trail of a bottle, from the growing of the grape to the final glass sipped by the consumer. Verified provenance not only proves the authenticity of a bottle, but can also trace how it has been handled and stored over time. 

Wine pros face the issue of handling and storage with stomach-churning consternation. Melissa Smith, founder of Enotrias Sommelier Services, describes how insufficient attention paid to such matters can be financially and even emotionally calamitous for buyers. 

“I worked with a collector who shipped $4 million worth of inventory across the country because they were moving,” Smith recalls, noting that she was not involved in the shipping decision. “It was supposed to be a safe shipping method for wine, with temperature control. But the truck’s refrigeration unit broke and everything froze. Bottles exploded, and the value of the wine was essentially wiped out. And it was only insured for $250,000. They got that, but it was devastating.”

While few stories of provenance gone awry are that dramatic, Smith notes that the industry has become increasingly serious about verifying provenance. “I’m finding more and more that top auction houses and retailers are requiring more proof of provenance, detailed storage conditions, and information on the collector than ever before,” Smith says. If any single circumstance is less than ideal—like storage conditions, or a handful of counterfeit bottles mixed in—an entire collection can be rejected, which costs everyone a lot of time and money. “When that happens, the integrity and therefore the investment in the collection vanishes,” she says.

Fighting Against the Fakes

In the late 1990s and early 2000s, a surge in counterfeit bottles made provenance more important, says David Parker, founder and CEO of Benchmark Wine Group, a leading source of fine and rare wine for retailers and collectors. “The more valuable and rare the bottle, the more important. For a collector, retaining purchase records is a key part of maintaining a provenance trail,” he says.

The best way to track and prove provenance, Parker says, is by making purchases directly from wine producers, on release from a licensed reseller, or from a very top retailer. For retailers, maintaining provenance is a headache. It entails recording the source and the buyer of every single bottle in the shop. Only a few retailers—like Benchmark Wine Group—do so. 

To ensure the provenance of the bottles they sell, Parker says they often inspect wine in situ to assure perfect storage: “Each bottle is closely hand-inspected. Every aspect from cork condition and position to fill level, wine color, label, capsule, and glass authenticity are closely observed.”

Each type of wine from each source is given its own SKU, which is then tracked during inventory, sale, and shipping. “Given our exhaustive vetting process, issues rarely arise,” Parker says. “Of the many tens of thousands of bottles we sell each quarter, only a handful are ever reported with problems. And in most cases, it turns out to be cork taint, which cannot be inspected for.”

Even with such clerical diligence in tracking provenance, other wine experts assert that close inspections and a paper trail don’t always provide an ironclad guarantee of quality. 

“Provenance may be primarily paperwork,” says Nick Kiniry, client advisor at the Washington, D.C. based World Insurance Associates. “But storage determines what the wine becomes and what it’s worth in the end. The higher the value of the bottle, the more stringent the risk management is going to be for us and the underwriter of insurance.”

Monitoring the conditions of a wine’s handling and storage remains very difficult, given the longstanding yet antiquated tools most wine pros are working with. Kinry believes that might soon improve: “We’re getting close to being able to utilize AI to scan a bottle and assess where it’s been, and how it has been stored and handled.”

The flipside is equally plausible though: AI can just as easily create fake labels and documents, including plausible records, invoices, and correspondence “documenting” the alleged provenance of a bottle. As AI becomes more sophisticated, distinguishing a real  from a fake document will be increasingly difficult. It’s already happening in the art world.

The Movement to Trace Provenance Digitally

As for tools that can help ensure the traceability and veracity of goods, there’s a lot of buzz in the wine industry—as well as others—about blockchain technology. In simple terms: A blockchain is a mathematical structure for storing data. It is shared across a network of computers, which is constantly monitored to ensure it hasn’t been changed, and that all copies of the record are the same. Blockchains are difficult to fake and are most frequently used to track cyber-currencies like bitcoin, but are also used to track an increasing number of valuable goods, from wine to art. 

Asher Rubinstein, a trust and estates attorney who works with high-net-worth individuals as a partner at Gallet Dreyer Berkey LLP, says that the technology is actually here, it just isn’t widely deployed because of the slowing of sales in recent years. “Implementing blockchain technology has taken a backburner as producers and importers focus on selling their wines,” Rubinstein says. “An industry-wide investment in blockchain technology just won’t happen until the downturn resolves itself.”

But when it does? Game on, Rubenstein says. “The blockchain stores all types of information like harvest conditions and composition of a blended wine, how much time it spent in oak, and more,” he says. “A sensor on a bottle can take temperature and humidity information and convey it on the blockchain, along with, for example, when that bottle was transferred from importer to distributor to retailer.”

Other wine pros, like Parker, are less convinced because it’s not a complete or comprehensive solution. “While it’s being used by at least one reseller in Europe to authenticate unique bottlings, blockchain tracking generally ends at shipping to customers, when the token gets ‘burned,” he says.

Companies like Enotek and ConnectedFresh, which offer sensors and integrated platforms to help producers, retailers, and collectors monitor storage temperatures, are still very up-and-coming, and aren’t widely integrated along the blockchain. 

Furthermore, Parker argues that blockchain technology is impractical for tracking wine provenance at scale because all but the rarest vintages are handled and sold by the case, not by individual bottles. “Opening such a case breaks the blockchain tracking,” he says. “Only by including deep investigation into ownership and storage, as well as extensive inspection for quality, can wine be tracked into and out of private commercial cellars by the bottle.”

No matter how it’s tracked, whether by arcane technologies or by good old-fashion pen and paper, provenance tells the story of a wine, of its journey from grape to glass, and its authenticity. To verify authenticity (a true luxury in our current era of the artificial), wine enthusiasts and serious collectors alike should, as much as possible, buy wine from known sources with strict provenance protocols in place. 

This ensures that your wine’s life has been as pampered and drama-free as possible, and thereby increases the chance that your wine will tell a story you actually want to hear.

title: We Found the Best Wine for Every Type of Girls’ Night
summary:
Whether you're seeing a show or hosting a mom hang, these wines recommended by our Tasting Department will match the vibe.

The post We Found the Best Wine for Every Type of Girls’ Night appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Whether you’re hunkering down for a cozy girls’ night in or going full on GNO, ideally there is some wine involved. Maybe it’s a happy hour carafe of crispy Muscadet, sipped slowly on a sunny summer sidewalk, or an Aperol spritz at a rooftop bar with another round on the way.

If that’s not your vibe, then maybe it’s a tart and textured orange wine to pair with the latest episode of Love Island, or a rich Cabernet Sauvignon, decanted as a hearty stew simmers and dinner party guests begin to arrive. The options are truly endless. From slumber parties to nights on the town, there’s an ideal wine for every type of girls’ night.

We tapped industry pros to give us a rundown on their go-to wines for these hangs. And of course, although we’re talking about girls’ nights, these wines are for anyone and everyone. So, if any of this sounds like a good time to you, grab a glass and your best friends, and get to gabbing.

Park Hangs with Grenache Blanc

“I’m all for a girls’ summer evening in the park: there’s no time limit, everyone brings what they like, and there’s generally good people-watching to keep the conversation going. I brought a very cold Garnacha Blanca and we all fawned over the texture. Even unoaked, these wines still carry plenty of body—something that reminds you of a fat, meaty green olive or thick-cut potato chip, which incidentally are great pairings with this zesty, salty, verdant wine.

Also known by the French name, Grenache Blanc, these wines often combine a distinct green, herbal element—think fennel and dill—that beautifully accentuates the fruity green apple, Asian pear, and honeydew notes. They’re not typically high acid, but racy citrus rind and deliciously lingering minerality keeps them balanced. These are substantial wines that are often pretty good value, perfect for an effortless evening kicking back outside.” —Ella Bennett, Wine Enthusiast’s client services & special projects coordinator

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Château Paul Mas 2024 Parcelle Belluguette Grenache Blanc (Languedoc)

Golden in the glass, this bottling is somehow both delicate and ripe, pairing aromas of nectarine and honey with lemon wedge and chamomile. There’s an oily and macadamia nut element to the palate that’s cut with citrus spray and stonefruit flavors. 93 Points — Matt Kettmann

$24 The Winery

French Bliss 2024 Grenache Blanc (Alexander Valley)

This bright and high-toned Grenache Blanc delivers aromas of tart pineapple, stone fruit and flowers on the nose. The palate is acid-driven, with loads of floral character, mouthwatering acidity and a bit of phenolic grip on the finish. 91 Points — Tom R. Capo

$39 Maslan Wines

All-Day Gatherings with Txakoli

“A few weeks ago, when a far-flung friend came to New York for a visit, she gathered femmes from our back-in-the-day crew for an extended hang in the neighborhood where we all cut our teeth together. As the afternoon stretched into evening, we traded our iced coffees and matchas for glasses of Txakoli, the lightly spritzy white wine from Spain’s Basque region.

To me, it’s the perfect wine for day-to-night summertime get-togethers: it’s bright and fun with a low enough abv to keep the party going. Plus, it pairs beautifully with cheese and charcuterie boards, tinned fish, and all sorts of salty, shareable snacks.” —Emily Saladino, Wine Enthusiast writer at large and reviewer of Croatia, Georgia, Greece, Hungary, Lebanon

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Inazio Urruzola 2023 Inazio Urruzola Txakolina White Hondarrabi Zuri (Getariako Txakolina)

Fresh, vibrant, with layers of aroma and flavor, this is a crisp, lightly effervescent white wine from the Basque region of Spain. A delightful example of Txakolina with firm quince squeezed over with lightly salted lemon picking up white herbs and light pith through the finish. Mouthwatering, a start for any meal. Editors’ Choice. 92 Points — Elaine Chukan Brown

$30 Flatiron Wines

Península Vinicultores 2022 Vino Atlántico Txakoli Hondarribi Zerratia (Bizkaiko Txakolina)

An attractive balance of layered aromas, a mineral, mouthwatering palate, and a greater complex of flavor than sometimes seen from the variety. Mixed citrus and pith, crisp orchard fruit, and a muddle of blanched almonds sprinkled with salt keep the palate refreshed, compelled for another sip. Enjoy with a mix of seafoods from lighter appetizers, to lobster risotto. 93 Points — E.C.B.

$25 Westgate Wine

Mom Hangs with Dry Riesling

“My fellow moms count on me to be their pocket sommelier when we gather, and I happily oblige. Sometimes I fall back on crowd-pleasing styles like bubbles or rosé, but I also enjoy introducing them to something new. Riesling is arguably the least understood grape variety in the world outside geeky wine circles.

There’s so much fear surrounding sugar levels. So I love to crack open a bottle of Australian or New Zealand Riesling where the typical style is bone-dry and ultra-refreshing with a beautiful sense of purity and place. It gets the conversation flowing and quenches everyone’s thirst at the same time. A win-win!’ —Christina Pickard, Wine Enthusiast writer at large and reviewer for Australia, New Zealand, England, and New York

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Rieslingfreak 2025 No. 33 Riesling (Clare Valley)

All the hallmarks of Clare Riesling are here: lovely floral, citrus, lemongrass, green tea and lamp oil aromas start. There’s a rush of rapier acidity on the bone dry palate that might be a bit much for those used to their Rieslings on the sweeter, richer side, but this reviewer loves the perky, zesty thrill of Riesling made in this style. It’s a bargain to boot. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — Christina Pickard

$18 Binny’s

Zephyr 2024 Riesling (Marlborough)

Riesling is a variety too rarely seen in New Zealand and that’s a crying shame. Zephyr’s version—just 10% alcohol—offers lovely purity and delicacy via lime leaf, orange blossom, chalk and a hint of spice. The mouth waters from the fresh, bright acidity and the textural weight implies food friendliness to boot. Drink now and over the next several years. 92 Points — C.P.

$14 Gary’s

Potluck and Comedy Show with Rosé or Chilled Red

“Once a month, a group of friends and I meet up for a potluck of sorts with a spectrum of ethnicities represented—African-American, Filipino, Haitian, Mexican—and heritage-based recipes as the highlights. I am frequently tasked with the wine selection for the evening and will often choose rosés or chillable reds. Because a full palate of flavors and spice levels are presented, I find these wines are most palatable to my friends’ likings. 

One of my favorite and most well-received bottles was a red New York state hybrid, Chambourcin, that took well to a slight chill. It was fun and fruity with moderate tannins and zesty acidity. Typically, not many of my friends venture beyond the ubiquitous grapes: Chardonnay, Merlot, Pinot Grigio, etc. So it was quite fun to expose them to a hybrid grape that was surprisingly well-received. While one bottle would usually satisfy the evening, I brought two bottles this time and was disappointed I didn’t bring more! After the potluck, we headed to our favorite comedy spot in Harlem and ended the night with laughter.” —Cheron Cowan, Wine Enthusiast writer at large and reviewer of Michigan, Indiana, Kentucky, Tennessee, Mississippi and the East Coast (excluding New York)

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Center of Effort 2025 Estate Rosé (Edna Valley)

This blend of 67% Grenache, 24% Syrah and 9% Mourvèdre is one of the best rosés of the year, its soft subtle pink hue leading into aromas of lemon rind and orange pith on the nose. There’s a fine line of acidity to the palate, which cuts through the compelling peach and melon flavors. 94 Points — M.K.

$40 Center of Effort

Samuel Louis Smith 2024 Baytree Lane Vineayrd Gamay Noir (Sonoma Valley)

This young Central Coast superstar headed north for Gamay this vintage, and the results fall in line with his lithe style. Quite transparent in the glass, the wine pops on the nose with wet stone and white pepper aromas that decorate the racy core of strawberry water and raspberry granita. The palate is vibrant, spicy, refreshing and, ultimately, a whole lot of fun. 94 Points — M.K.

$33 K&L Wine Merchants

Italian Dinner with Conversation-Starting Bottles

“There are so many styles of wine that lend themselves to a fun night out. My best girls’ night out with my BFFs run the gamut from me playing sommelier at the table to us just ordering randomly what we can share and drink copious amounts of. 

Recently, we ended up at an old-school Italian restaurant. The surprise was the dynamic selection of wines from not just Italy but local and domestic offerings. Our conversation was centered on the bounty of aromatic, fresh, lively otherworldly wines being produced in California, Oregon, New York, and Texas. The pricing was fair and encouraged sharing more than one bottle.

Our choices for the evening were Falanghina, Fiano, Barolo, older California Cabernet Franc, and various Nebbiolo grown in other locations around the world. The thought was fresh, lively, quenching, crushable, chilled wines to pair with seafood, poultry, meat, and cheeses.” —Tonya Pitts, Wine Enthusiast writer at large and reviewer of California (Northern California & California AVA), Arkansas, Colorado, Illinois, Kansas, Missouri, Nebraska, Nevada, Oklahoma, and Utah

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

La Guardiense 2024 Alfabeto – Janare Falanghina (Falanghina del Sannio)

The nose has the white flower and lemon scent of fresh laundry. That same element defines the palate, but notes of lime and honey add nuance and create a mouthfeel which is not only chalky, textured and substantial, but also fresh and citrusy. 92 Points — Danielle Callegari

$13 Michael’s Wine Cellar

Jacuzzi 2023 Furvum Nebbiolo (Petaluma Gap)

The buoyant and charming nose of this amphora-aged Nebbiolo displays lovely black fruits, olives and flowers, while the palate displays grippy tannin, balanced acidity and dark earthy flavors of blackberry, cranberry, sage, chopped herb mélange and black licorice. 93 Points — T.R.C.

$65 Jacuzzi

title: This Maximalist Jewelry Trend Has Roots in Prohibition
summary:
As evidenced by the year’s highest profile fashion events, cocktail rings are back and bling-ier than ever. But what do they have to do with cocktails?

The post This Maximalist Jewelry Trend Has Roots in Prohibition appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
After this year’s Met Gala, bold cocktail rings emerged as one of the evening’s standout jewelry trends. Gala co-chair Nicole Kidman flashed a cocktail ring featuring a ruby center stone surrounded by diamonds. Zoë Kravitz, Chase Sui Wonders, and Stevie Nicks also sported cocktail rings, while Rihanna flashed three statement diamond sparklers on her hands. 

The on-trend bling made plenty of appearances at the Oscars, SAG Awards, Grammys, and fashion events around the world. But even outside of A-list affairs, bold cocktail rings are a growing trend, as understated minimalism falls out of favor. And, yes, they really do have a connection to cocktails.

A Fashion Trend with Prohibition Roots

What exactly is a cocktail ring? In general, it’s a ring with a very large center stone, often adorned with smaller diamonds or other stones, while an engagement ring is often a single stone. 

They’re intentionally flamboyant and meant to attract attention. “A cocktail ring is almost like a hot fudge sundae of a ring,” says Diana Singer, president of the American Society of Jewelry Historians. “It’s somewhat dome-shaped, usually large, incorporating several different colors and shapes of stones.”

Initially, cocktail rings were accessories that women purchased for themselves, rather than received from fiancés or romantic partners. As a result, the dramatic, oversized rings became a symbol of rebellion and financial independence for women. 

“Cocktail rings first came into vogue in the 1920s, during Prohibition,” when sales of alcohol were outlawed, but private cocktail parties kept the drinks flowing, explains Nicola Nice, author of The Cocktail Parlor: How Women Brought the Cocktail Home and a forthcoming book about the history of cocktail hour. “Much like the short dresses of the flappers and long strings of pearls, they were a statement. But the original statement was a subversive one.”

The Cocktail Connection

At the time, alcoholic beverages were taboo in the American mainstream, and so was independence for women. But the wheels of progress were in motion: in 1920, the 19th Amendment gave women the constitutional right to vote. Meanwhile, growing numbers of women were entering the workforce, giving many financial independence for the first time, and automobiles promoted greater mobility (literally and figuratively) away from hearth and home. Social mores were changing, too: it became acceptable for women to socialize—and drink—unchaperoned.  Taboos were swiftly unraveling, and the cocktail ring became a particularly rebellious symbol.

“It was a piece of jewelry that draws attention to the fingers and the hands, and what was in the hands,” Nice says. “This was during Prohibition, a moment when you weren’t meant to be consuming alcohol, and wearing a piece of jewelry that draws attention to this.”

According to the International Antique Jewelers Association, women intentionally wore these rings on the right hand, often on the index finger, so it wouldn’t be mistaken for an engagement or wedding ring. When ordering a fresh drink, a flapper would raise her right hand, flashing her ring for attention, the IAJA says; some even matched the color of the stone in their ring to the color of their favorite cocktail.

It’s not a coincidence that glittery cocktail rings came into vogue just as many women embraced cocktail culture, Nice observes.

“Before Prohibition, we hadn’t had cocktails be glamorized in the same way, that they become an accessory,” she says. “The glassware becomes more ornate, more dainty, more feminine, at the same time that the cocktail becomes more democratized among men and women. You had women grasping at something that up until that point was much more of a man’s domain, and making it their own and more importantly, making it beautiful.”

In other words? “Accessorizing yourself to the moment—and the moment being designed around the cocktail—is something really special and powerful.” 

Cocktail rings fell out of favor during the lean years of the 1930s and 1940s wartime. World War II also brought restrictions on the importation of colored precious stones like rubies, emeralds, and sapphires, notes ASJA’s Singer. Jewelry styles became more restrained.

In the 1950s and ‘60s, cocktail parties returned as a way to socialize. Cocktail rings made a comeback too, as precious gemstones became more readily available.

“During the post-World War II boom, when there was so much affluence in the U.S., it was important for the middle class to show they had arrived at a certain level of financial comfort,” Singer says. For women, that included hosting or attending parties, wearing beautiful cocktail dresses, and flaunting jewelry, particularly an opulent, easy-to-spot ring: “It was a way of exhibiting one’s affluence and sophistication.”

One More Round

The cocktail ring has returned once again. Celebrities are embracing oversized silhouettes and dramatic gems and continue to do so elsewhere in the fashion world; experts predict that will become a rising trend, as bold jewelry replaces understated pieces.

“Minimalism has dominated in fine jewelry the past few years,” observes Irina Aran, founder and CEO at Facets Fine Jewelry. “Think: delicate stacks, dainty necklaces, and barely-there bands.” 

Now, maximalism has returned, she continues. Right now, people value bold pieces, particularly vintage and estate rings that carry a story, or trinkets dramatic enough to invite in-person commentary or conversation—a radical analog shift when so much connection happens via screens. 

The cocktail, however, is optional.

“Cocktail rings are about confidence,” Aran says. “You don’t wear it to be subtle. You wear it because you walked into the room and decided the room should know you were there.”

title: The New Age of Wine Has Begun—Just Ask the SuperVinoBros
summary:
WE 2026 Rising Stars Ryan and Chris Goydos, better known as the SuperVinoBros, are leading the charge of new-age wine advocates who champion sustainability and approachability.

The post The New Age of Wine Has Begun—Just Ask the SuperVinoBros appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
For twin brothers Ryan and Chris Goydos, better known as the SuperVinoBros, wine was never meant to be treated as a private language. What began during the pandemic as two brothers from New Jersey filming themselves tasting and learning about natural wine has become one of the wine world’s most engaging social media platforms. Their videos are informative but rarely self-serious, and their willingness to get things wrong, particularly during their blind tastings, is central to their appeal.

That openness has helped the brothers connect with different generations of wine drinkers. Younger viewers recognize the fast, informal language of social media, while more experienced drinkers respond to their genuine curiosity and growing knowledge. At a moment when the wine industry is struggling to attract new consumers, the SuperVinoBros offer an encouraging example of how wine can be discussed without pretentiousness or intimidation. For that reason, among many others, Wine Enthusiast named the brothers to our 2026 Rising Stars list, which you can read both online and in our recent Rising Stars print issue.

In this episode of the Wine Enthusiast Podcast, I speak with Ryan and Chris about SuperVinoBros’ inception, why they think it took off, and how their relationship with wine, and their audience, has evolved. We discuss Ryan’s recent trip to Bordeaux with NBA star and passionate wine collector Jimmy Butler, as well as how the escalating prices of Bordeaux and Burgundy have made many of the world’s most celebrated wines increasingly exclusive. We also look ahead to the future of wine communication, exploring what greater inclusivity in wine can look like, what traditional wine media still gets right, and how social media is changing the way wine knowledge is shared.

Listen to learn more about the two brothers helping wine find a new audience.

On Balancing Approachability with Seriousness

Ryan Goydos: “I think it’s kind of like… you wanna be thoughtful about the wine you’re drinking, right? I think that for us, you know, the way we always—well, the way I absorb information, I think the way Chris does as well, is that I need to know everything about what I’m drinking because I think it’s interesting, right? And so I think that—I will give full credit to Chris, I think he’s a really talented writer and he’s able to make all these scripts that feel very approachable and quick and punchy and stuff. But I think just putting information that’s interesting but also important to the story of the wine is what we try to focus on. 

… But then on the flip side, it’s like, okay, now we just open the wine and let’s see what we think about it. Like we… the thing about us is that we never try all the wines we feature. We’ve never tried them before, for the most part, and we have no idea what it will be like. And we’re just kind of going into it blind. We’re kind of going on this journey with the people that are watching the video too. The analogy I always say is, ‘You gotta eat your vegetables first before going to dessert,’ right? You gotta learn a little bit about the wine before you open the wine, right? Because you want to be a little intentional about how you consume it. So I think that kind of juxtaposition of education versus just hanging out and drinking wine is what we try to strive for in videos. And I, at least, hope that people think that makes it feel a little more approachable and accessible, you know?”

On What Being Named a WE ‘Rising Star’ Means to Them

RG: “It is surreal, and it’s honestly such an honor and a privilege to be on a list of such incredible wine professionals. I think that when Chris and I started this, we were like, ‘We don’t know anything about wine’ and, ‘We’re just learning ourselves and we just want to have fun with it,’ right? But you know, growing up, we were like, ‘You need to be a sommelier to know anything about wine,’ right? And so I think it’s really gratifying and so, so exciting to be recognized as a Rising Star when we’re just trying to do our best to self-teach ourselves, you know? So I think it’s an honor, it’s really an honor and a privilege, honestly.”

Chris Goydos: “Yeah. And to kind of build off of that, I think that, more than the personal gratification that we get from being recognized, I’m happy that our vision and our message is being recognized as well. You know, the fact that wine is not dying. Wine is bigger than ever and it’s fueled by a younger generation that’s more interested in it than people understand.”

Check Out Our YouTube Channel

On Visiting Bordeaux with NBA Star Jimmy Butler

RG: “So it’s a really funny story and I’ll keep it brief because it can be as long as I can make it. But essentially, Jimmy, I did not know this, so Jimmy is a fan, was a huge fan of us, or is a huge fan of us. I’m in California for a wedding and on the way home, basically just, like, one morning, Jimmy Butler just DMs us and is like, ‘Yo, when are we hanging out?’ And I’m like… I thought the message was fake, you know? ‘This is, there’s no way. This is like, this is spam, right?’

And I open it up—lo and behold, it’s Jimmy Butler, and it was real. I was like, ‘This is crazy.’ And so, I won’t even get too long-winded about that, but basically he invites us to his place in Southern California. We hang out, we open up a bunch of crazy bottles, and he goes… at one point in the night after like a couple bottles deep, he’s like, ‘Ryan, like I’m actually going to Bordeaux at the end of July. I’m not sure if you’re free, but you know, keep your calendar open if you want to join.’ And I was like, ‘There’s no way this guy’s being serious. He’s just being polite. We’re a couple bottles deep, like, there’s no way this is happening.’

And around like mid-July, I was like, ‘You know what, let me just ask him… let me see if he’s serious still. And I text him like, ‘Hey Jimmy, I’m free the last week of July if there’s still a spot.’ And he was like, ‘Yeah, actually there is a spot, Ryan…. Buy your ticket and we’ll figure out the rest.’ And before I knew it, I was flying to Paris and took a train to Bordeaux at the end of July and was just hanging out, hitting all these crazy first growth domains in Bordeaux. It was very, very surreal, truly. It was… I think Jimmy is, like, the most genuine, coolest, most thoughtful person, celebrity I’ve ever met, and seeing him talk about wine the way we talk about wine—like honestly, he’s echoing everything we say or we’re saying right now on this podcast. He’s like ‘wine’s meant to be shared. Let’s open up the bottles.’ Like ‘who cares about collecting?’ Like ‘just open them up.’ It’s so cool to see someone of that, you know, those accolades that he has to have that same mentality as all of us, being like, ‘Yeah, let’s just open up the wine.’ Like ‘drink your wine.’ Like ‘open up ‘82 Petrus,’ ‘Open up, you know, Screaming Eagle blanc’… you know? So I think that that was a really cool mentality I think he has.”

On Whether Burgundy and Jura Are Inaccessible

CG: “So Burgundy and Jura… what I like about both of them, because even though Burgundy’s a little bit more, you know, people consider it ‘conventional’ wine, there are still young winemakers doing really cool experimental things there. And I think that Burgundy, in general, cares a lot about their soils, their terroir, their vineyards, their Grand Cru sites. They’re very intentional about the way that they make their wine. Jura—very similar. I don’t think that the producers are necessarily to blame. You know, I think that what ends up happening is you get this culture of allocation where people buy up the wine and therefore make it inaccessible… I think the difference here is that—I think that there’s many, at least not everybody, but there are definitely some people in Bordeaux and some people in Burgundy and some people in Jura that are intentionally trying to be exclusive.

But I think for the most part, the young winemakers and the exciting winemakers there don’t necessarily want their bottles to be impossible to buy. And I think it’s more so—this is all anecdotal—but more so a product of a secondary market and more so a product of hoarding and collecting rather than sharing and drinking.”

RG: “I agree with you, Chris. And also to that point, I think it’s a lot of speculation sometimes, right? Like you have these young winemakers that are coming up, they’re like, ‘Hey, I can make wine in Burgundy and sell it for a crazy amount of money and make a ton of money…’ Not to say that it’s all about money, but you know, you’re seeing the speculation with like—I mean, one example is William Kelley, right? Like these wines are thousands of dollars before even they’re being released, right? Like they’re… Tino Kuban, another great example, right?

And so I think that this speculation market and this kind of collecting, like Chris said, definitely kind of makes Burgundy inaccessible sometimes, which, you know, makes you nervous. But I think the… and honestly I’m glad you asked that question too, Aleks, because, like, we just had a Burgundy tasting event, like a new-age Burgundy event with La Paulée back in early July, and the whole idea was just to promote cool, young Burgundy producers, or not even young, just like cool, natural Burgundy producers that are trying to make wine the right way and trying to keep it at a price point that’s accessible, right?

Like I think the wines that we love are like… the (François de) Nicolay wines…. Those wines are awesome, right? And they’re pretty affordable and they’re clean and they’re consistent and they’re great, and then they’re at a price point that isn’t too egregious, right? So I think Burgundy’s always gonna be like, you know, inaccessible to a certain degree. Like you’re always gonna have the Romanée-Contis, like the stuff that just is so super inaccessible. But I think there’s always… I think what excites me about Burgundy is that… in Jura as well, like this kind of youth movement of like cool wines that are being produced by thoughtful people that are trying to make wine still feel affordable.”

On the Future of Wine and Wine Media

RG: “I think in terms of what the wine scene is gonna look like … I think, unfortunately, the one thing we need to look at is climate change, right? I think that that’s really gonna change the landscape of what industries look like or, sorry, what regions look like for anywhere in the world in five years, honestly, right? Like, you know, there’s massive heat waves in France right now that are like… people have to pick now, which is insane to think about. We’re in mid-August and people are, you know, almost done with their harvest in certain places. And so I think that will really—”

Aleks Zecevic: “Yeah. I just wrote an article about the fires in Spain, in Gredos, and one of the very good points that one of the winemakers brought up is, like, you can’t think of the terroir in the same way after the fire has destroyed all these things around us. So, anyway, sorry to interrupt.”

RG: “Yeah, it’s crazy. No, no, no. I think it’s such a good point. Like these winemakers need to fundamentally change the way they look at their land and their grapes and their harvest, right? And so I think that number one will dictate anything we drink in the future, right? And so I think that’s one point that needs to be in consideration.

But also, like, the optimism I have is that, you know, I think more and more regions, as they get more spotlight, we’ll continue to have producers that get propped up and continue to kind of make names for… like one example is Styria, like you brought up, Aleks. A region like that, I think, is only gonna get more and more attention and spotlight because people are gonna start realizing, ‘These wines are really good’ and they are at a price point that feels a little less offensive than maybe a Burgundy is, right? Or a region like the Rheinhessen or the Mosel where you’re making incredible, incredible wines, super undervalued. And I think that people are gonna continue to look into regions that have that accessibility, whether that’s access or price or any of that….

Again, I think we all love French wine, right? But there’s so much more to the world than just French wine, right? Like Chris and I just had a Verdejo from the north of Spain that tasted like Jura Savignin. I was like, ‘This is insane. This is… who’s making wine like this?’ That’s exciting. And that exploration is honestly what continues to push us. And so I hope that that’s where the industry goes moving forward and then I’ll let Chris comment on the other part of that because the second question’s also really important too.”

CG: “To echo Ryan’s point, the future of the industry is, you know, figuring out where all the next big regions are gonna be. I feel like we were always trying Eastern European or Central European wine and that’s, you know, places that were really only farming vineyards for like the last twenty to thirty years. And then now they’re finally coming out with amazing expressions of the terroir. There’s a whole new world in that regard. Not even just in Europe, but also like South America and the United States, Canada, making really, really interesting wines that are still pretty much under the radar.

But I think in terms of the second part of the question, in terms of wine media and what that looks like, Ryan brought up a good point the other day. Like the Michelin guide just recently dropped their Grapes [list]… there’s all sorts of wine media popping up all over the place, you know. And I think that what that says to me is that the media industry is starting to realize that wine is coming back in a very big way.

For the last, you know, 10, 20 years, every headline you read about wine is, ‘people aren’t drinking wine anymore. The wine industry’s dying. People are selling off their vines.’ Like, ‘why is no one drinking anymore?’ And I think that everyone who’s interested in wine and everyone that loves drinking wine has always known that wasn’t really true… Maybe it’s alarmist, maybe it’s getting clicks and headlines, but I think wine media is finally starting to realize that wine is coming back in a very big way. And, you know, whether that looks like traditional media, like print media, or it looks more like social media the way that me and Ryan have been doing it, you know, it’s hard to say. But I will say that the powers that be are realizing that wine is not dead and it’s coming back in a very, very big way.”

On the Future of SuperVinoBros

CG: “The short term goal is to get a blind correct. That’s my short term goal. But I think the long term goal is… you know, me and Ryan, when we first started this, never imagined it would be the community that it is today. But I think, if anything, I want SuperVinoBros to be a voice, to continue to be a voice and continue to be kind of a champion of, you know, the new age wine movement… I want us to be that voice that is saying, ‘Well, the conventional wine scene as we know it might be dead, but the new age of wine and sustainability and being intentional about consumption, that’s all just begun.’ So that, to me, no matter what we do in the future, I want us to continue to be that voice.”

AZ: “Ryan, anything to add?”

RG: “Yeah, no, a hundred percent. I think Chris said it really beautifully. I think that—just continuing to spread the good word, right? I think that there’s always more people every single day, every single week, you know, there’s always new people that engage with our videos or engage with us in our DMs or in person that are just like, ‘I’m getting into wine now and your content is helping me do that,’ right? And that brings both of us so much joy. And so I think again, what that looks like in the future, you never know, but I think that we’re just gonna keep moving with a lot of intentionality with, again, telling the stories that excite us and kind of spreading the good word that is natural wine and wine consumption. Because I think it’s such a fun world to be a part of and honestly the more people in here, the merrier.”

The Guests

Ryan and Christopher Goydos are twin brothers and the founders of SuperVinoBros, a wine media company focused on making wine more approachable and fun to explore. Through travel, tastings, education, and storytelling, they highlight the winemakers, regions, and bottles shaping wine culture today. Together, they’re helping introduce a new generation to wine through curiosity, accessibility, and a fresh perspective.
