CG

Nah, I think, I do think that it is funny. You know, I think like the content strikes a nerve, like it resonates rather, with both like younger and older wine drinkers in a way, you know. And I think that the new wine fans, again, I think that, me being one of them, right, resonate with the movement of taking wine back from mass production and taking wine back from, you know, large, large companies and more so making, you know, what was intended to be like a cultural, agricultural product that, you know, is meant to be shared by the world. I think that older wine drinkers that have become disillusioned with the wine industry because of what it’s become in the last couple of decades, you know, find the new wine wave as refreshing. And not only that, but they also like to see that the younger generation is getting interested in something that they were… that they’re passionate about.

So, you know, I think that we probably do strike a chord with older and younger wine drinkers. Though I will agree with Ryan that I think that the majority is younger.

AZ

You just mentioned, and I think this is a very interesting topic because you mentioned kind of like this accessibility, and you know that wine is a beverage that is meant to be shared by the world, right? And I think we are all witnesses that certain wines are, you know, unreachable for certain people, if you’re not in the wine community, if you’re not in the industry, or also if you’re just financially not, you know, you can’t afford it.

This is a problem. What do you think about this? We actually kind of had this as one of the questions for you guys for the rising star article, which we’re gonna get into later, but I wanted for you guys to answer for the podcast.

CG

So… definitely a very loaded question because this has been a problem probably forever in the wine world, right? Like allocations and not being able to like… the best of the wine world is always gonna be closed off. Whether it’s financial barriers, you don’t have the right access to the right people to purchase it, it’s always been that way. And even in the new age of wine, the natural wine world, there are still unicorn bottles that you can’t obtain, you know, or that are impossible to obtain. And I think that, what we try to do with our content, especially in certain videos, now we have friends who are in the wine scene who resonate with our message of being inclusive and not gatekeeping wine, who will actually give us access to some of these bottles with the hope that we’ll open them on camera and share them with the rest of the world, in a way.

So we—the first time that I really felt that was when we were able to get some Domaine des Miroirs out of the Jura for the grand finale of our Jura series, which is, you know, any natural wine fan will know that’s like a unicorn bottle. That’s like, creme de la creme, can’t get it anywhere else. And, we were able to get it because of a generous friend of ours in the wine industry who said, “wine’s meant to be drank,”you know, “I’ll only give this to you if you promise me you’re gonna open it and then record it.”

Thankfully a lot of other people have followed suit since then. So that’s part of our content that I really enjoy is being able to un-gatekeep stuff like that and kind of get past that mentality that wine belongs in the cellar aging, it actually is meant to be open and enjoyed.

RG

Yeah.

AZ

Did you get a lot of messages about the Domaine des Miroirs? People asking how they can get it?

CG

There was actually one guy… there was one bottle we opened, I can’t, I’m gonna butcher the name, but there was one bottle we opened. It was this really rare bottling. Like this one guy made only like five thousand bottles of it and we recorded it. Once again, very similar story, like somebody in the industry gave us access to it so that we can record it. And the winemaker messaged us saying like, “Wow, thanks so much for the great feature. Where did you find this, by the way?” Like you can’t find this anywhere. Like the winemaker himself is saying that.

So, and yeah, to answer you, long story short, yes, a lot of people are always very excited that “wow, you guys got you guys got this one. That’s awesome.”

RG

Yeah. But also Aleks, like to that point, I really, like, love what you said initially in the beginning as well. Just like “wine is meant to be shared.” Like I think, and maybe we can dive into it more later, but like this idea of, like, wine community and wine culture is something that we were exposed to as we started to get more into natural wine. Like you go to like the wine fairs and salons of the world, like Le Dive and Karakterre and Printemps right and Champagne and all these things are literally just people, or herds of wine enthusiasts that are just opening up

insane bottles of wine and just pouring it for strangers on the street sometimes, right? And I think that mentality of sharing and camaraderie and community is really, really rare to find. And I think it’s a really special thing about this wine community that has only propelled us even more forward of being like, “wow, we’ve been shown so much generosity and about people showing us bottles, and we just want to do our best to kind of spread the word as best as we can,” you know.

AZ

I totally agree with that. That’s… I think that’s why I also enjoy it very much.

RG

Yeah.

AZ

I wanted to also discuss—you’ve been named the Rising Stars by Wine Enthusiast. And I wanted to ask, what does this recognition mean to you guys?

RG

Yeah, no, I mean, I truly like… it is surreal and it’s honestly such an honor and a privilege to be on a list of such incredible wine professionals. You know, I think that when Chris and I started this, we were like, “We don’t know anything about wine and we’re just learning ourselves and we just want to have fun with it,” right? But you know, growing up, we’re like, “you need to be a sommelier to know anything about wine,” right? And so I think it’s really gratifying and so so exciting to be recognized as a rising star when we’re just trying to do our best to self-teach ourselves, you know. So I think it’s an honor, it’s really an honor and a privilege, honestly.

CG

Yeah. And I think that, you know, to kind of build off of that, I think that more than the personal gratification that we get from being recognized, I’m happy that our vision and our message is being recognized as well. You know, the fact that wine is not dying. Wine is, you know, bigger than ever and it’s fueled by a younger generation that’s more interested in it than people understand.

AZ

Totally. I wanted to ask, Ryan: what felt more surreal, this or hanging out with Jimmy Butler?

RG

Haha, both are just as surreal, honestly, I would say.

AZ

No, no, you don’t have to answer. You don’t have to answer that question. But what you can do actually is, why don’t you tell us a little bit about the experience? It was… you hung out with him at the World Cup first, but then you also went to Bordeaux, right? I just got your newsletter.

RG

Sick. Thank you for reading the newsletter. That’s great. Yeah, no, so it’s a really funny story and then I’ll keep it brief because it can be as long as I can make it. But essentially, Jimmy, I did not know this, so Jimmy is a fan, was a huge fan of us, or is a huge fan of us.

AZ

Okay.

RG

And and so, you know, I’m in California for a wedding and on the way home, basically just like one morning, Jimmy Butler just DMs us and is like, “Yo, like when are we hanging out?” And I’m like… I thought the message was fake. You know, I was “This is, there’s no way. This is like, this is spam, right?” And I open it up, lo and behold, it’s Jimmy Butler, and it was real. I was like, “This is crazy.” And so, like, won’t even get too long-winded about that, but basically he invites us to his place in Southern California. We hang out, we open up a bunch of crazy bottles, and he goes… at one point in the night after like a couple bottles deep, he’s like, “Ryan, like I’m actually going to Bordeaux at the end of July. I’m not sure if you’re free, but you know, keep your calendar open if you want to join.” And I was like, “there’s no way this guy’s being serious. He’s just being polite. We’re a couple bottles deep. Like, there’s no way where this is happening.”

And around like mid-July, I was like, “you know what, let me just ask him.” Let me just follow up with him on WhatsApp. Or let me just text him, see if he’s serious still. And I text him like, “hey Jimmy, like I’m free, you know, last week of July if there’s still a spot.” And he was like, “Yeah, actually there is a spot, Ryan.” Like “buy your ticket and we’ll figure the rest.” And before I knew it, I was flying to Paris and took a train to Bordeaux at the end of July and was just hanging out, hitting all these crazy first growth domains in Bordeaux. It was very, very surreal, truly. It was in… honestly, and into that point, like I think Jimmy is like the most genuine, coolest, most thoughtful person, celebrity I’ve ever met.

And seeing him like talk about wine like the way we talk about wine—like honestly, he’s like echoing everything we say or we’re saying right now on this podcast, he’s like saying the same thing. He’s like “wine’s meant to be shared. Let’s open up the bottles.” Like “who cares about collecting?” Like “just open them up.” And like it’s so cool to see someone of that, you know, those accolades that he has to have that same mentality as all of us being like, “yeah, let’s just open up the wine.” Like “drink your wine.” Like “open up ‘82 Petrus,” open up, you know, Screaming Eagle blanc, open up this. It’s like “let’s enjoy it.” You know? So I think that that was a really cool mentality I think he has.

AZ

I think it’s also interesting because you know, you said earlier that you started with the natural wine community and then now you went with Jimmy Butler to visit the first growths, which are probably not in the natural wine community. So I wanted to ask you about this experience and these wines. And also, Chris, if you wanna chip in, I don’t wanna keep you out of the conversation, but…

CG

I unfortunately was left out of this party. So I… Ryan can speak to the experience itself. I have my own opinions about that though in general. You know, I think that when you walk into a wine shop, especially asking for like, you know, natural wine, even if it’s a conventional wine shop, a lot of the people that work there will kind of scoff at you, right? And they’ll be like, “Yeah, you guys will never experience,” you know, “my biodynamically farmed handpicked grapes that DRC is.” We’re talking about the same kind of wine here. You know what I mean? It’s like: good wine is good wine. It doesn’t… just cause it’s not labeled natural doesn’t mean it’s not good wine. So– but I’ll let Ryan speak more specifically about his experience at the first growth.

RG

No, I think honestly Aleks, I’m glad you asked the question because, like, I think Bordeaux is a really interesting topic when we’re talking about wine, especially with the way people consume wine now, right? Like I think Bordeaux, and I think I’m not the only one that has this opinion, I think a lot of other people share this opinion, that like they really shot themselves in the foot with their marketing, right? Like the bottles are too inaccessible, it feels too buttoned up, it’s all white tablecloth kind of situation, right?

And so a lot of drinkers, including me and Chris, were super…

CG 

Disillusioned.

RG

Disillusioned, right? We’re like, “there’s no way we can even think about these bottles, so why would I even learn about Bordeaux?” Like “I don’t even care about Bordeaux, like I will never be able to drink this, so I I’ll go to Loire Valley, I’ll go to the Rhone Valley, I’ll go to Jura.” And so I think that that positioning, I mean, whether it was intentional or not, like really hurt Bordeaux, right? Because now there’s a lot of excess wine, of wines from Bordeaux, right? There’s, you know, people are ripping up vines now and no one’s drinking it, sales are going down. And I think that it’s a really interesting use case of like where the flaw of like making wine too inaccessible does to a region. And so what I really enjoyed when I went to Bordeaux, I would say, because I agree with you completely, like it’s definitely not natural wine, especially in certain places, that there’s a lot of people that recognize kind of the missteps that were taken kind of by previous generation and they’re trying to kind of reconcile that, right? I think one of the greatest, the best examples I can give is that Chateau Lafite Rothschild has a new woman that’s leading the charge. It’s – her name’s Saskia DeRothschild, and she’s like super big into like biodynamic farming now. Like she’s trying to convert the vines of Lafite Rothschild into biodynamics and sustainability.

And I think again it’s… I’m sure there’s a long way to go. You know compared to like some of the wines that we drank in terms of their biodynamic practices, but at least they’re thinking about it. And I think seeing that was really encouraging because before I went to Bordeaux, I was like, “I don’t really… I don’t really care that much about…” like I mean, obviously I know they’re really special and like these wines are coveted for a reason, but like “I can’t really resonate or relate to these wines at all.” And so going there kind of gave me a really cool perspective of being like, “okay, like they recognize that there’s been some missteps in the past and they’re trying to kind of reconcile and fix kind of what the image they—or the image they’ve been painted in the past—and then trying to fix that. So I think that was a really cool perspective to get.

AZ

I think Haut-Brion is also biodynamic from what I… I’m not 100% sure, but I think so. But no, I totally agree. And you bring up a very important point. Inaccessibility shoots you in the foot at some point. And do you think that Burgundy is going that same direction? Because really, when you look… like I’ll give you an example. I remember in 2016, I was in Trier in Germany, my first ever professional trip to Germany. And I had a wine from Bizot that was 70 euros on a restaurant menu. That same wine today is in retail, if you can find it, like 3,000, so at a restaurant is more. You know, and that’s, again, if you can even find it.

RG

Yeah, that’s crazy.

AZ

So I have to ask you what you guys think about Burgundy, but also to an extent Jura as a, let’s say, natural wine pioneering region. Is Jura also going in that direction?

CG

So Burgundy and Jura, which… what I like about both of them, ’cause even though Burgundy’s a little bit more, you know, people consider it “conventional” wine, there are still young winemakers doing really cool experimental things there. And I think that Burgundy in general cares a lot about their soils, their terroir, their vineyards, their Grand Cru sites. They’re very intentional about the way that they make their wine. Jura—very similar. I don’t think that the producers are necessarily to blame. You know, I think that what ends up happening is you get this culture of allocation where people buy up the wine and therefore make it inaccessible. So I don’t think that the… I think the difference here is that I think that there’s many, at least not everybody, but there are some, there are definitely some people in Bordeaux and some people in Burgundy and some people in Jura that are intentionally trying to be exclusive.

But I think for the most part, the young winemakers and the exciting winemakers there don’t necessarily want their bottles to be impossible to buy. And I think it’s more so, this is all anecdotal, but more so a product of a secondary market and more so a product of hoarding and collecting rather than sharing and drinking.

RG

Yeah. No, I agree with you, Chris. And also to that point, I think it’s a lot of speculation sometimes, right? Like you have these young winemakers that are coming up, they’re like, “Hey, I can make wine in Burgundy and sell it for a crazy amount of money and make a ton of money.” Or making really good wines, right? Not to say that it’s all about money, but you know, you’re seeing the speculation with like I mean, one example is William Kelly, right? Like these wines are thousands of dollars before even they’re being released, right? Like they’re… Tino Kuban, another great example, right?

And so I think that this speculation market and this kind of collecting, like Chris said, like collecting market definitely kind of, you know, makes it very makes Burgundy kind of inaccessible sometimes, which, you know, makes you nervous. But I think the… and honestly I’m glad you asked that question too, Aleks, because like we just had a burgundy tasting event, like a new age burgundy event with La Paulee back in early Julym and the whole idea was just kind of promote cool, young burgundy producers, or not even young, just like cool natural burgundy producers that are trying to make wine the right way and and trying to keep it at a price point that’s accessible, right? Like I think the wines that we love are like… Nicol… the was it Nicolai, Nicolet? Like the the Nicolai wines—

AZ

François de Nicolay.

RG

Nicolay, thank you. Those wines are awesome, right? And they’re pretty affordable and like they’re clean and they’re consistent and they’re great, and then they’re at a price point that isn’t too egregious, right? So I think Burgundy’s always gonna be like, you know, inaccessible to a certain degree. Like you’re always gonna have the Romanee Contis, like the stuff that just is so super inaccessible. But I think there’s always… I think what excites me about Burgundy is that there’s some like, in Jura as well, like this kind of youth movement of like cool wines that are being produced by thoughtful people that are trying to make wine still feel affordable.

CG

Yeah.

AZ

Jura hasn’t gotten to the point where the wines are, I mean, apart from maybe like five wineries, wines are not like extremely expensive. It’s more the difficulty of finding them. And that’s also kind of like a thing that just happened with the harvests and the weather there. It’s not that easy. But you brought up a point earlier about, you know, people buying up and stocking. I think both of you actually brought it up. You’re basically saying that you think that the reason why they keep it and then they kind of like hype it up is because they invest in these bottles as they would invest in stock? So for example, if I bought Apple stock, I would tell all of you guys that Apple is the best, obviously, because I want my stock to go up.

CG

Yeah. That’s a solid point. Yeah. And I think for sure it kind of goes along with the whole commoditization of wine in general, where it’s less about what’s in the bottle and more about, you know, what you can get for it. Obviously money’s always gonna rule all, you know, I understand that, I think it’s a solid point that the assigned value of the bottle itself is not necessarily representative of how good the wine is. And I think that at the same time though, that also makes it fun to seek out so-called undervalued bottles, usually places that aren’t in France, that like, can taste just as good as a burgundy, right? But, they just don’t get the same recognition because of the region that they’re in or the country that they’re making wine in. So on the one hand, I do think that that’s like, you know, I think it’s I think it’s a solid point that, you know, artificial… assigning artificial value to bottles is certainly something that I can see happening. It makes it cool to try to explore bargains and things that actually… wines that taste just as good, if not better, that just aren’t recognized.

AZ

No, totally. I mean, also when you go to… when you see vineyards, I don’t know, in the Mosel, that are like seventy percent inclined, very hard to work, you have to work by hand. I mean, or in Styria where people would regularly die in tractor accidents. And then you go to Burgundy, that is rolling hills. It’s, you know, it doesn’t look as… you really, like, question yourself. But of course it’s a supply and demand thing.

But to that point, what do you think the wine industry will look like in five years? I feel like there’s some huge changes happening at the moment in terms of pricing, availability, wine styles. So I feel like the natural wine has become kind of mainstream, and some people are now even going away from it. You know, will Burgundy be in the same situation as Bordeaux? Will the price start going down? Like, what are your thoughts on the future of the industry, but also what do you think the wine media industry is gonna be like in five years?

RG

Two awesome questions. Definitely have two, I think, very different answers. But I think in terms of where the wine scene is gonna look like, I think it’s… truly, I think unfortunately the one thing we need to look at is climate change, right? I think that that’s really gonna change the landscape of what industries look like or, sorry, what regions look like for anywhere in the world in five years, honestly, right? Like, you know, there’s…

AZ

Absolutely.

RG

Massive heat waves in France right now that are like… people have to pick now, which is insane to think about. We’re in mid-August and people are, you know, almost done with their harvest in certain places. And so I think that will really—

AZ

Yeah. I just wrote an article about the fires in Spain, in Gredos, and one of the very good points that one of the winemakers brought up is, like, you can’t think of the terroir in the same way after the fire has destroyed all these things around us. So, anyway, sorry to interrupt.

RG

Mm-hmm. Yeah, it’s crazy. Yeah.

No, no, no. I think it’s such a good point. Like these winemakers need to like fundamentally change the way they look at their land and their grapes and their harvest, right? And so I think that number one will dictate anything we drink in the future, right? And so I think that’s one point that needs to be in consideration. But also like the optimism I have is that like, you know, I think more and more regions, as they get more spotlight, we’ll continue to have producers that get propped up and continue to kind of make names for… like one example is Styria, like you brought up, Aleks. Like I think a region like that, I think, is only gonna get more and more attention and spotlight because people are gonna start realizing, like, “these wines are really good” and like they are at a price point that feels a little less offensive than maybe a burgundy is, right? Or a region like yeah, like the Rheinhessen or the Mosel where you’re making incredible, incredible wines, super undervalued. And I think that people are gonna continue to look into regions that have that accessibility, whether that’s access or price or any of that. And so I think yeah hopefully… my hope is that you start to promote more regions that are exciting to drink from, not just, again, I think we all love French wine, right? But there’s so much more to the world than just French wine, right? Like Chris and I just had like a Verdejo from the north of Spain that tasted like Jura Savignin. I was like, “this is insane. This is… like who’s making wine like this?” That’s exciting. And that exploration is honestly what continues to push us. And so I hope that that’s where the industry goes moving forward and then I’ll let Chris comment on the other part of that ’cause the second question’s also really important too.

CG

No, yeah. To echo Ryan’s point, the future of the industry is, you know, figuring out where all the the next big regions are gonna be, I feel like we were always trying like Eastern European or like Central European wine and that’s like, you know, places that were like, really only farming vineyards for like the last like twenty to thirty years. And then now they’re finally coming out with, amazing, you know, expressions of the terroir. There’s a whole new world in that regard. Not even just in Europe, but also like South America and the United States, Canada, making really, really interesting wines that are still pretty much under the radar. But I think in terms of the second part of the question, in terms of wine media and what that looks like, Ryan brought up a good point the other day. Like the Michelin guide just recently dropped their… their Grapes. I don’t know if that is what they’re calling them, instead of Michelin stars.

RG

The grape guide, yeah, like Michelin grapes or whatever, yeah.

CG

Grapes, right? There’s all sorts of wine media popping up all over the place, you know. And I think that what that says to me is that the media industry is starting to realize that wine is coming back in a very big way. For for the last like, you know 10, 20 years, every headline you read about wine is, “people aren’t drinking wine anymore. The wine industry’s dying. People are selling off their vines.” Like, “why is no one drinking anymore?” And I think that everyone who’s interested in wine and everyone that loves drinking wine has always known that wasn’t really true. And it might…  maybe it’s alarmist, maybe it’s getting clicks and headlines, but I think wine media is finally starting to realize that wine is coming back in a very big way. And, you know, whether that looks like traditional media like print media or it looks more like social media the way that me and Ryan have been doing it, you know, it’s hard, it’s hard to say. But I will say that, the powers that be are realizing that wine is not dead and it’s coming back in a very, very big way.

AZ

Yeah, I totally agree. And I think, if anything, I think consumers are just looking with a little more intention at what they’re drinking and, you know, not to put any wines down, but I think there are too many wines out there that lack character, so people just don’t care about those wines anymore. And then we’re looking at the numbers of, you know, a traditional winery that’s been producing tens of millions of cases a year, and their numbers are dropping, surely, but we have to also look at, you know, the smaller craft producers. You wanted to say something, Ryan? Sorry, I—

RG

No, I think I just, again, just kind of emphasizing and echoing honestly both of the things that you guys are saying. Like I think there’s a real movement of intentionality when it comes to consumption in all aspects, right? Like, you know, whether it’s the food you make for dinner or the wine you drink, right? Like I think that the focus on small production, anti-industrialization, anti-commercialization is where the wine industry is. And I think a lot of consumers… what excites me the most is that a lot of consumers, I find, are being a lot more thoughtful about the wines they pick and the wines they’re pouring in their glasses, right? Like you’re right—nothing against these big bulk wineries, because I’m sure they’re, you know, a majority of people still drink them and they really enjoy them. But I think, you know, when we’re talking about wine that’s good for the planet, and obviously alcohol’s not good for you, but if you’re gonna drink something, you might as well drink something that’s gonna make you feel good. Like that category of wine is, I think, only increasing.

And what excites me about that category, especially with media, is that more people are talking about it, right? The more people talking about it, and sharing this knowledge with the masses, the better. Because I think, again, I would imagine you feel the same way, Aleks. But like Chris and I, nothing makes us happier than to see people enjoying the wine that we like too. Like I get so much joy when I’ve taken friends to Le Dive for the first time or I’ve poured them a really cool wine from Styria and they’re like, “What is this?” Like “this is insane.” Like, “how have I never realized this existed,” right? And so it’s kind of like, you show somebody this world that is natural wine or this kind of approachable wine world, and they’re hooked, right? So I think the more and more people talking about it is only better for the industry.

AZ

Absolutely. All right. We’re gonna start wrapping it up, but I’m gonna ask you one last question, and that is how do you see your role in the next years? What do you… are you gonna change anything? You’re gonna keep doing the same thing? I know Chris is becoming a doctor soon.

CG

That’s one part of it. I think the next thing is to race to see if I finish residency first or I get a blind tasting right first. We’re—

RG

Ha ha ha.

CG

We’re still working on that. So, you know, that, to me, the short term goal is to get a blind correct. That’s my short term goal. But I think the long term goal is, you know, I don’t know what exactly this is gonna look like, me and Ryan when we first started this never imagined it would be the community that it is today. But I think if anything, I want SuperVinoBros to be kind of a voice, to continue to be a voice and continue to be kind of a champion of, you know, the new age wine movement and understanding that, you know, I want us to be that voice that is saying, “Well, the conventional wine scene is as we know it is might be dead, but the new age of wine and sustainability and being intentional about consumption, that that’s all just begun.” So that, to me, is, no matter what we do in the future, I want us to continue to be that voice.

AZ

Ryan, anything to add?

RG

Yeah, no, a hundred percent. I think Chris said it really beautifully. I think that just continuing to spread the good word, right? I think that there’s always more people every single day, every single week, you know, there’s always new people that engage with our videos or engage with us in our DMs or in person that are just like, “I’m getting into wine now and your content is helping me do that,” right? And that brings both of us so much joy. And so I think again, what that looks like in the future, you know, you never know, but I think that we’re just gonna keep moving with a lot of intentionality with, again, telling the stories that excite us and kind of spreading the good word that is natural wine and and wine consumption because I think it’s such a fun world to be a part of and honestly the more people in here, the merrier.

AZ

Right, guys, nice to see you, and thank you for joining the podcast.

RG

Thank you so much, Aleks. Appreciate it.

CG

Thanks so much, Aleks.

AZ

Check out more from our Rising Stars Issue in print and online at wineenthusiast.com. Subscribe to this podcast on Apple, Spotify, and anywhere else you listen to your favorite shows. You can also go to wineenthusiast.com/slash podcast for more episodes and transcripts. I’m Aleks Zecevic, and thanks for listening.

title: Don’t Leave Peru Without Tasting the Potato Wine
summary:
In the mid-2010s, a Peruvian farmer and winemaker came up with a way to preserve native tubers. Enter: potato wine, a creamy, mildly sweet beverage taking Peru by storm.

content:
I’ve never met a potato that I didn’t like, whether blanketed in cheese or crisped and then sprinkled with sea salt. So it was no surprise that I loved eating my way through Peru, a country that boasts over 4,000 varieties of tubers and an array of potato-based dishes, such as papa a la huancaína, taters dressed in a sauce made with ají amarillo chilis and queso fresco, and papa rellena, mashed spuds molded around a stuffing of minced meat and then deep fried. But one iteration of my favorite root vegetable that I never expected was potato wine, a beloved yet unconventional take on traditional wine with a unique backstory. 

My introduction to potato wine started with a stay at Sumaq Hotel, a luxurious riverside hotel at the base of Machu Picchu. Its on-site restaurant, Qunuq (meaning “warm” in the indigenous Quechua language), specializes in regional delicacies, such as carpaccio-style alpaca meat and locally-foraged vegetables smoked in a pachamanca (otherwise known as an “earth pot”), an underground pit used to cook ingredients with heated stones. But what really commanded my attention throughout the hotel’s six-course Flavors of the Andes tasting menu was a potato wine pairing. 

Exclusive Access to
Wine Country,
Led by Wine Enthusiast

The potato wine was pale and cloudy in appearance and bore little resemblance to mainstream grape varietals. It also had a creamier, thicker mouthfeel, much like sake or even a hearty vodka, and tasted nutty, mildly sweet, slightly herbaceous, and—no surprise—earthy.  Other bottlings more closely resemble traditional wine, like the Malbec-like red made from black-skinned Mashua Negra.

“Rather than being a traditional wine, it is a modern interpretation of ancient Andean ingredients,” explains Omar Saravia, Sumaq Hotel’s food and beverage director. “Throughout the Andes tubers and native potatoes have been cultivated and valued for centuries. Today some producers are taking these ingredients to a new level through innovative artisanal fermentation techniques.”

From Ground to Glass

As Saravia explained to me, the concept of potato wine is fairly new. In the mid-2010s, Manuel Choqque, a Peruvian farmer, chef, winemaker, and agronomist engineer, came up with a way to preserve native tubers that were at risk of disappearing, while also transforming them into something delicious. Most potatoes lack the natural sugars required for fermentation, but he found success with a sweet-enough species: Oxalis tuberosa, a colorful root vegetable native to the Andes. 

Choqque makes and bottles this fermented drink in Huatata, a rural community near Cusco (the traditional gateway city to Machu Picchu), about 3,700 meters above sea level. The production process is closer to that of sake, with a multi-step process of sun-curing, cooking, must extraction, slow fermentation, and maturation in its extreme, high-elevation climate. Traditional sun-curing can take 20 to 60 days to increase natural sugars, reduce acidity, and develop fruity aromatic profiles, though it is never rushed or overlooked due to the method’s ties to sacred Incan traditions. 

Of course, the beverage is not technically a “wine” in the strictest sense—as it doesn’t include grapes—though the parlance has taken off. Choqque produces his inventions under the labels Miskioca, after oca and miski, the Quechuan word for “sweet,” and Oxalis, after the species’ genus. Its nuanced flavor profile, dictated by fermentation methods and subtle differences in oca, make it a challenging yet exciting meal companion, one that native chefs are keen to work with. Saravia of Sumaq Hotel says that Choqque’s bottles are most commonly found in restaurants, tastings, and special gastronomic experiences that showcase authentic Peruvian products and culinary heritage.

A Food-Friendly Wine That Isn’t Meant to Be Scaled

“Potato wine pairs exceptionally well with Andean cuisine—roasted vegetables, mushrooms, corn, [other] tubers, and meats such as alpaca or lamb,” Saravia tells me. “It has a smooth and distinctive texture that helps balance dishes with intense flavors or those heavily focused on vegetables or proteins.” 

Wildly variable, potato wine often has a “surprise with every sip” element, but this inconsistency has been embraced by cooking talent who ultimately allow the land to dictate the final tasting experience. 

Though the drink can be enjoyed at many bars and restaurants in Peru, don’t expect it to make a stateside debut. “Cultivating and improving these native plants demands a great deal of time, labor, and investment, which keeps volumes low and costs high,” Saravia says. Because the beverage category is quite young and still largely unknown outside of the Andes, there’s an “education curve” to its consumption before international drinkers understand what they are tasting. 

Moreover, production requires an artisanal, small-batch approach: It takes roughly eight to ten kilograms (roughly 17 to 22 pounds) of Oxalis tuberosa to make a single liter. “The tubers must be sun-dried and double-cooked before pressing, and the extreme high altitude climate makes fermentation slow, lasting three to four months,” Saravia explains. “That alone limits how much can be made in a year.” And because these bottles are technically “fermented tuber beverages” rather than grape wines, exporting internationally involves navigating label and regulatory questions that conventional exports don’t face. 

“For now the focus is on quality and on telling the story through tastings and high-end restaurants, rather than on scaling volume,” Saravia says. “The priority is to protect the character and origin of the product.”

Potato wine represents the intersection of biodiversity, culture, and innovation. Whether or not it gains global appeal is beside the point. Its regional identity and elusiveness is what makes each pour special, educating adventurous palates and celebrating the humble root vegetable and its influence on Peruvian food culture. And as someone whose body composition is always part potato, to that I say “cheers.”

title: Texas Wine Deserves All the Hype
summary:
As quality becomes the priority, many Texas growers are experimenting with new ways to express the region’s diverse terroir.

The post Texas Wine Deserves All the Hype appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The word “Texas” probably reminds you of barbecue, beers, burgers, and big steaks. Certainly, the state has its fair share of all of those. But more and more, Texas is becoming a hub for wine and wine tourism, with well over 500 wineries operating across eight AVAs. 

Amazingly, over ninety percent of Texas wine is consumed within the state. Many wineries are small family affairs that champion the local scene, while others are larger scale operations working with both Texas fruit and fruit from other areas. 

One thing is for sure: the buzz building around this burgeoning wine scene is well earned, as the quality of Texas wines has never been better.

The Region

Texas is big. No secret there. Like any wine-growing area, the vineyards are concentrated in just a few key spots around the state. The majority of wine grapes come from the high-altitude plateau known as the Texas High Plains. 

This AVA is the second largest by area in the state, and despite having just a few wineries located there, it’s the viticultural powerhouse. The Texas High Plains are generally flat, and situated between 3,000 and 4,000 ft. in elevation, which is higher than most other American Viticultural Areas. Wind and altitude drive the quality of the grapes here. If you’ve had Texas wine recently, it was likely grown in this AVA.

By way of comparison, the vast majority of Texas’ producing wineries are located in the slightly lower elevations of the Texas Hill Country AVA, near the city of Fredericksburg. It’s here that the splendor of Texas wine is on full display, with gorgeous large-scale tasting rooms and intimate salons where wine lovers can experiment. The scene is on par with Napa Valley or Sonoma in the heady days of the early 2000s: think modern tasting facilities with full-blown restaurants and striking architecture. Tour buses, Insta stories, and bachelorette parties abound, but this area also possesses more dramatic topography and complex soil arrays that many winemakers feel are the future of Texas wine. In other words, Texas Hill Country isn’t just about the scene.

The Climate

Texas is hot. No secret there, either. 2022 and 2023 saw pretty intense drought conditions, with 2024 returning to more average rainfall and more moderate (but still pretty darn hot) summer temperatures. Importantly for grape growers, the diurnal shift here is smaller when compared with other prominent wine regions. Daytime temperatures in the summer are very warm, and overnight temperatures don’t drop nearly as much as in some parts of California or Oregon. The result in both Texas Hill Country and the Texas High Plains is a relatively short and occasionally volatile growing season. Winemakers see a compacted harvest schedule, as they attempt to juggle the schedule of picking, transport, and fermentation for a very diverse set of varieties.

The Grapes

As quality becomes the priority, many growers here are experimenting with new ways to express the region’s diverse terroir. And there lies the excitement around Texas wines. The possibilities seem endless as growers play with a wide range of varieties, from everyday classics to more obscure grapes that perform admirably in the local conditions. Here’s a recap of the Texas wines that have stood out in our blind tasting sessions over the past year.

Bright Whites:

Picpoul Blanc is the buzzy white in Texas at the moment. This higher-acid variety delivers a pop of freshness that just resonates here. These examples are great for pairing with shellfish or just sipping on hotter days.

Lost Draw Wines 2024 Timmons Estate Vineyard Picpoul Blanc (Texas High Plains)

This focused and zippy Picpoul Blanc delivers punchy aromas of lime, tart pineapple, ginger, and citrus blossoms on the nose. The palate vibrates with zesty citrus acidity and packs a punch of fresh green herbs, tropical fruits, and white flowers. 91 Points — Tom R. Capo

Inquire with the winery

Kerrville Hills Winery 2023 Picpoul Blanc (Texas High Plains)

Zippy aromas of apple skin, toasty spice, and white flowers drive the nose of this Picpoul Blanc. The palate is rich and creamy, with plush texture, bright Meyer lemon acidity, and flavors of roasted pear, ginger, and wildflowers that wrap up a clean finish. 90 Points — T.R.C.

$32 Vinoshipper

Richer Whites:

Other Rhône varieties have shown great potential in Texas as well. These more structured versions provide some richness and opulence that can handle grilled fish or other heavier courses.

K Estate 2024 Estate White Blend (Texas Hill Country)

This blend of Marsanne, Roussanne, and Albarino delivers aromas of tart pineapple, green pear, honeysuckle, and nectarine on the nose. The acid driven palate brings pithy texture, and flavors of pomelo, lemon verbena, white flowers, and candied ginger through the finish. 90 Points — T.R.C.

$40 Health Family Brands

Hilmy Cellars 2022 Canted County Vineyard Marsanne (Texas High Plains)

This zippy and fresh Marsanne brings aromas of lively citrus, fresh cut flowers, and crystalized ginger on the nose. The palate feels broad and neatly balanced with pithy lemon-lime acidity and flavors of fresh Gala apple, lemon verbena, and apple blossoms through the finale. 91 Points — T.R.C.

$28 Hilmy Cellars

High-Altitude Iberian Grapes:

The high plateaus of Texas are very reminiscent of Rioja, where altitude and wind shape the style of the wines. That fact means that varieties from Spain and Portugal make loads of sense here (not to mention the possibilities for pairing with grilled meats).

C.L. Butaud 2021 Tempranillo, Farmhouse Vineyards Tempranillo (Texas High Plains)

The nose of this Tempranillo sings with aromas of pure cherry, spiced raspberry and purple flowers. The palate brings more of that red fruit energy and more aggressive potpourri and herb flavors that linger and expand on the palate. 92 Points — T.R.C.

Inquire with the winery

Signor Vineyards 2020 Estate Touriga Nacional (Texas Hill Country)

This bright and lifted Touriga Nacional brings rich raspberry, cocoa and violet aromas on the nose, with darker berry, plum, cedar and cinnamon coming through on a palate with focused acidity and rich tannin. The finish lingers with echoes of malt, bitter chocolate and sage. 92 Points — T.R.C.

Inquire with the winery

Italian Style:

Italy is notorious for its vast array of regional grape varieties that aren’t well known on the global scene. Many of these are hearty, full-bodied varieties that beg for rich cuisine. In Texas, some of these are gaining a following for good reason.

Hilmy Cellars 2021 Veeart Vineyards Montepulciano (Texas High Plains)

Dark berries, licorice, violets, and cracked pepper drive the nose of this charming Montepulciano. The palate deftly balances ripe acidity and plush tannin, framing flavors of roasted cherry, plum, and cocoa through the finale. Drink this with hearty pasta on a cold night. 91 Points — T.R.C.

$60 Hilmy Cellars

Perissos Vineyard and Winery 2022 Aglianico (Texas Hill Country)

Aromas of dark berries, herbs, and cracked pepper highlight the nose of this Aglianico. The palate has a deep malty richness, plush tannin, and flavors of baked cherry, fig compote, chocolate, and cinnamon through the finish. 91 Points — T.R.C.

$60 Perissos Vineyard and Winery

Kerrville Hills Winery 2021 Teroldego (Texas High Plains)

Punchy aromas of dark berries, black cherry, chopped herbs, and toasty spices explode from the glass of this Teroldego. The palate is rich and textured, with juicy acid balancing forceful tannin and flavors of crushed blackberry, cherry, plum, sandalwood, and a sanguine note that lingers with nuances of roses at the finish. 90 Points —T.R.C.

$30 Vinoshipper

French and Food-Friendly:

French grapes that thrive in hotter climates have been successful here in a variety of styles. From the crushable, chillable Cinsault to ageworthy Tannat, these are some bottles worth seeking out.

Meredith Margaret Wines 2025 Cinsault (Texas High Plains)

The nose of this gently extracted Cinsault erupts with the aromas of Morello cherry, violets, and cinnamon. The palate mingles bright acid with crunchy tannin, dancing the line between Rosé and chillable, quaffable red, giving flavors of fresh cherry, lime peel, and flowers. Chill and serve poolside this summer. 91 Points — T.R.C.

$24 Rivenburgh Beverage Company

Kerrville Hills Winery 2023 Tannat (Texas Hill Country)

The nose of this Tannat delivers a punch of black fruit and savory herb aromas, giving way to flavors of roasted meats, black plum, salty earth, black pepper, and rose petal in a framework of powerful tannin. Decant this early and serve with grilled steak or lamb. 92 Points — T.R.C.

$40 Rivenburgh Beverage Company

Elisa Christopher Wines 2023 Amélie Bordeaux-Style Red Blend (Texas High Plains)

This Bordeaux-style blend delivers bright plum, dark raspberry, wildflower and herb mélange aromas on the nose. The palate is silky textured, with smooth tannin, fresh acidity, and flavors of baked cherry, cinnamon, milk chocolate, and violets that lift the finish. 91 Points — T.R.C.

$48 Elisa Christopher Wines

title: Europe’s Next Great Chardonnay Hotspot Is Not Where You Think
summary:
The real story isn't simply that German Chardonnay has become better. It's that it stopped trying to be something else.

The post Europe’s Next Great Chardonnay Hotspot Is Not Where You Think appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
For a week this spring, I reviewed more than 500 German wines, expecting Riesling to reaffirm why it remains the country’s defining white grape. Instead, somewhere between the familiar brilliance of Riesling and Germany’s increasingly accomplished Pinot Noirs, I found myself returning to Chardonnay.

Across Baden, Rheinhessen, the Pfalz, and beyond, quality was remarkably consistent. The wines combined freshness with texture, precision with generosity, and, perhaps most strikingly, all of the above with confidence. Having followed German wine for the past decade, I wasn’t surprised to find outstanding Chardonnay. What surprised me was how many producers had reached such an exceptional level.

The reasons why are both climatic and cultural. Warmer seasons have made ripening more reliable, while growers have become more exacting about where Chardonnay belongs. Older aromatic clones have given way to lower-yielding French selections, vineyards have matured, and a new generation of winemakers has returned from Burgundy and other wine regions with a sharper understanding of both vineyard and cellar.

“The vineyard is where great Chardonnay is made,” says Tobias Knewitz of Weingut Knewitz in Rheinhessen. “The cellar can’t create greatness, it can only preserve what the vineyard has already given us.”

That philosophy surfaced in nearly every conversation I had with German winemakers. Producers spoke of healthier soils, better site selection, spontaneous fermentation, longer lees ageing, and increasingly restrained oak. All are in service of expressing place rather than technique. Climate change has undoubtedly helped Chardonnay ripen more consistently in German wine regions, but it has also shifted the challenge toward preserving freshness while navigating frequent spring frosts.

Yet, after speaking with producers and sommeliers, I realized that the real story isn’t simply that German Chardonnay has become better. It’s that it stopped trying to be something else.

“We don’t want to make Burgundy in Germany,” Knewitz says. “We want to make Welzbachtal.”

The Next Great Chardonnay Producers

That confidence is increasingly evident in the glass. Rather than chasing richness or lavish oak, today’s German Chardonnays are defined by energy, tension, and transparency. Matt Turner, wine director at Lei Wine Bar in New York City, consistently finds, “a sort of flinty orange-citrus zest character” running through many of the wines. Chicago sommelier Zach Eastman describes the best examples as combining “an authentically Germanic taut acidity, tension, and minerality” with balanced ripeness and lightness.

There is no single German Chardonnay style, and that may be its greatest strength. “The thing about German Chardonnay is that it doesn’t have to be Burgundy, or Jura for that matter,” says Heather LaVine, owner and wine director of Golden Hour Wine and Quicksand Bar à Vin in Orlando. “It can be its own thing.”

Rather than sharing a rigid stylistic blueprint, LaVine believes the finest iterations are united by an almost unquantifiable sense of energy, one born from thoughtful farming, transparent winemaking, and an honest expression of place.

The cellar has changed, too. “When I was training, I sometimes wondered whether people actually liked Chardonnay or whether they simply liked oaky white wine,” says Carsten Saalwächter of Weingut Saalwächter.

Many modern producers allow fruit, texture, and site to take center stage. Saalwächter jokes that the higher phenolics in his wines give them an edginess, so “you don’t feel as though you’re drinking a lemon cheesecake.”

To appreciate the seriousness of German Chardonnay, “all one has to do is blind taste,” Turner says. I was reminded of that during a visit to Moritz Kissinger, one of Germany’s most exciting Chardonnay producers. Moritz and his wife, Jasmin, poured us a baker’s dozen Chardonnays from some of the world’s finest producers to taste blind. Germany more than held its own. 

It’s easy to see why: these are wines of precision, freshness, and quiet confidence, often offering remarkable value.

“Producing truly great Chardonnay is not the biggest challenge,” says Johannes Kopp of Weingut Kopp in Baden. “Convincing people that Germany belongs among the world’s top Chardonnay producers is.”

After tasting more than 500 German wines this spring, that’s an increasingly difficult argument to dismiss.

title: Is Wine as We Know It on the Brink of Extinction?
summary:
A recent study is sounding the alarm for historic wine regions, if something doesn't change immediately.

The post Is Wine as We Know It on the Brink of Extinction? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Toasting to love and milestones with a glass of Champagne is a relatively ordinary, if elevated and delightful exercise. But it may soon seem as quaint and lovely, but as rare and incompatible with contemporary life as churning butter at home. 

In France and Spain, major portions of wine country went up in flames this summer, echoing an all-too-familiar phenomena haunting countries around the world, every year. Hundreds of thousands of acres of land have been incinerated in Spain and France, with hundreds of thousands of people evacuated from their homes and land. 

When it’s not on fire, it seems like wine country is contending with a deep freeze. This year alone, vineyards across the East Coast and France were devastated by surprise spring freezes and hail events that devastated up to 90% of their potential harvest. If it’s not fires and ice, it’s flooding or drought.  

Direct threats to viticulture from extreme events have moved from once a century ordeals to annual nightmares. But scientists are warning that that harvest damage is the tip of the climate iceberg. A recent study published in Environmental Research Letters warns that it may be too late to save wine grapes—along with other luxury crops like coffee and chocolate—from extinction in some of the regions where they’re currently grown by as early as 2036, unless radical changes are implemented. 

How Climate Change Warps Grape Growth Cycles

While viticulturalists can’t control climate change, or the corporations and governmental policies that many experts warn are actively contributing to greenhouse gas emissions and causing extreme weather events, and an estimated $28 trillion in environmental damage, some researchers and viticulturalists are working to mitigate the effects of climate change they’re already seeing in the way their grapes grow and develop. 

“It’s the extreme heat that worries me most,” admits Jean-François Ott, fourth-generation winemaker at Domaines Ott in Provence. “Above a certain temperature, the vines stop functioning. When I was a child, the harvest began two to three weeks after school started. Today, my children are starting school and we’ve almost finished the harvest. We’ve lost more than a month in 40 years.”

The vine’s growth cycle, Ott says, is also accelerating. 

“We used to have 100 days between flowering and harvest, and today we’re down to 80 days,” Ott says. 

In the face of these stark changes—a reduction of 20% in the time a plant grows has serious implications for the quality of the final product—researchers are turning to geoengineering, like stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI), as a potential mitigation. 

“The main idea of SAI is to inject very small, very reflective sulfur dioxide particles into the atmosphere at about 70,000 feet,” says Ariel Morrison, Ph.D., who led the luxury crop study at Colorado State University. “This would create a hazy reflective cloud around the entire planet, which would reflect some sunlight away from the surface and cool the earth.”

Morrison and her colleagues used a climate model to simulate what might happen to temperature, rainfall ,and humidity during the period between 2036 to 2045. SAI can cause temperature to drop,  but it also redistributes heat, rain, and humidity, making it ineffective as a solution in 12 of the 18 major luxury crop regions they studied. Lower temperatures may slash heat stress, but the risk of early winter warmth followed by frost, can’t be guaranteed, which elevates the risk of budbreak damage. 

While Morrison would like to see SAI and other geoengineering solutions, like marine cloud brightening should be studied, she says that without “reducing greenhouse gas emissions” and implementing serious changes in farming practices, wine culture as we know it will be threatened. (Marine cloud brightening is exactly what it sounds like: sea salt particles are sprayed into low-lying marine clouds, which boosts their brightness and reflectivity).

“I think grapes will still grow where they’re currently planted, but whether they will thrive and produce high-quality wine is more questionable,” Morrison says. 

This very pressing problem is top of mind in wine country. 

“Today we’re facing heat levels—even at night—that are forcing us to significantly alter our methods,” Ott says. “Because it takes 10 years from planting to producing a high-quality harvest like the one we aim for, and it’s complicated to completely relocate a vineyard, we’ve significantly adapted our cultivation methods.”

He’s not alone. 

Rethinking Vineyards Spacing and Orientation 

Traditionally, vineyards have been planted to optimize sunlight. But in recent decades, the variety of climate extremes makes that a less sure gamble. 

Being prepared for “anything” motivated the complete replanting initiated at Gloria Ferrer Wines in Sonoma in 2014. They are replanting about 10 acres a year of the 330-acre organically farmed vineyard. 

“As we replant and redevelop our vineyard, we want to be prepared for everything,” says vineyard director Brad Kurtz. “We are purposefully doing everything we can to increase flexibility and long-term resilience.”

One of the biggest forms that’s taking is the team’s decision to change vineyard orientation. 

“We’ve had several crazy heat events that have caused sunburn on Pinot Noir,” Kurtz says. “By changing orientation, it protects the grapes from the harsh afternoon sun. And it coincides with the dominant wind direction, so after excess rain events, the wind dries grapes out and blows off potential disease.”

Adam Casto, head winemaker at Ehlers Estate in Napa, notes that he is currently in the midst of approaching “one of the earliest harvests in recent memory, currently projected to be about two to three weeks ‘early’ of ‘normal.’”

Casto blames the consistently drier, hotter climate conditions, but also “consumer and media trends, globalization, technology, labor, and more.”

Indeed, as wine lovers want fresher and less boozy wines, the climate wants to deliver the opposite. 

Like the team at Gloria Ferrer, Casto and his crew have modified the vineyard design to balance solar irradiance, heat, and water stress. In addition to adjusting row direction and spacing, Casto is experimenting with fruit height and canopy distribution. 

“We are several years into trials with an exciting experimental vine architecture that so far is showing great promise,” Casto says. “We also planted two pilot blocks of Marselan and Arinarora this year to begin learning what other cultivars might be useful in the future as components of our estate.”

Diversifying Grapes and Rootstocks

Experimenting with lesser known, indigenous grape varieties and more resilient rootstocks is a work in progress at many vineyards. 

In Rías Baixas, Spain, winemakers like Emilio Rodríguez Canas at Terras Gauda, are seeing earlier harvest dates consistently. This has pushed them to implement many changes, including seeking out longer-cycle grape varieties that will ripen at “normal” times amid accelerated growing seasons. 

“Caiño Blanco has become a standout variety at Terras Gauda thanks to its very long growing cycle,” Canas explains. “It buds shortly after Albariño and ripens considerably later. With such a long growing cycle, the final part of its ripening takes place in cooler weather with shorter days, which prevents over-ripening and the loss of acidity, important characteristics that have defined our wines for years.”

At Gloria Ferrer, Kurtz says they’ve explored a variety of clones and different rootstocks for their Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, in the hopes of finding great resilience to heat stress and drought. They’ve also created an experimental sparkling Pinot Blanc, brought in Chenin Blanc, and considered using Malvasia Blanc. 

Extreme weather is a bigger problem than early harvests in Mendoza, says Alejandro Vigil, winemaking director at Catena Zapata and co-owner of El Enemigo. And because “every vintage asks different questions,” diversification of everything has become the name of the game. 

“Rather than relying on one solution, we match each variety and farming practice to the specific environment,” he says, noting that their vineyards range from 400 meters to 1,700 meters above sea level. “More than 80% of our Malbec vineyards are planted with massal populations, rather than a single clone. Those populations contain a wide range of genotypes and phenotypes, creating natural diversity within the vineyard. It becomes an insurance policy against uncertainty.”

(Vineyards) Climbing Every Mountain

Insurance is good. 

For every 100 meter increase in elevation, the average temperature decreases by between 0.65 and 1 degrees Celsius. So if a vineyard is 1,000 meters above sea level, it will be up to 10 degrees cooler than a vineyard at sea level. 

Nicolas Catena, Vigil notes, began raising the elevation of vineyards decades ago, before discussing changes in the weather became the opposite of boring. That diversity of vineyard sites, with differences in temperature, solar radiation, water availability, and ripening conditions, allows him to still harvest healthy crops in many places, whether the vintage is hot, cold, dry, and / or wet. 

And while Morrison finds the prospect of higher-elevations promising, she notes there is a built-in limit to the exciting innovation. 

“Expanding to higher elevations or latitudes, which may have previously been too cool to grow grapes, is another option to mitigate the effects of warmer temperatures,” she says, alongside other worthy changes, like planting heat-tolerant grapes and shading vines. “Grapes need a certain amount of sunlight for photosynthesis and polyphenol production, so there’s a limit to the elevation and latitude at which grapes can grow.”

Morrison is also concerned that many of the most impactful interventions are expensive and impossible for smaller producers. She also noted that according to their projections, the likelihood “frost death,” after warm winters produce early buds, which are then demolished by a spring frost, are highest in France, Germany, and northern Spain. 

“Grapes may still generally thrive in these regions, but there could be more years when unexpected frost death wipes out most of a year’s crop,” Morrison says. 

That kind of harvest damage was seen in parts of Europe this spring, with climate’s other vandal, wildfires, finishing the job in France and Spain in July. Grapes will almost surely survive. But their ability to be grown and fermented into something we want to toast to our greatest achievements with will require deep innovation, care, and commitment to sometimes uncomfortable, expensive change. It needs to start now, if not yesterday.

title: How Fires Ravaged One of Europe’s Most Exciting Wine Regions
summary:
The wildfires that swept through Spain's Sierra de Gredos have forced a reckoning on the future of winemaking.

The post How Fires Ravaged One of Europe’s Most Exciting Wine Regions appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
When Gearóid Lane finally understood what the fire had done to San Gregorio, there was little left to romanticize.

The vineyard, tucked into the pine forests above El Tiemblo in Spain’s Sierra de Gredos, had vines dating to the 1920s. It was one of the sites around which Lane and his partners built Bodega El Reventón, and the source of one of their two single-vineyard wines. By the time the flames passed, much of the surrounding forest was black and the vineyard had suffered heavy damage.

Still, Lane believes most of the vines will survive.

“With lots of love, hard work, and investment, we will be able to nurse the great majority of the San Gregorio vines back to health,” he says.

Gredos was hardly alone in watching the horizon burn this summer. In late July, enormous fires west of Bordeaux forced mass evacuations and came unnervingly close to one of the world’s most famous wine regions. Bordeaux’s principal appellations escaped direct fire damage, but smoke, extreme heat, and drought have added another layer of uncertainty ahead of an already unusually early harvest.

Days later, the wildfire threat shifted east. Greece battled major fires around Athens and elsewhere in early August, yet another reminder that Europe’s wine regions are entering an era where fire is becoming an increasingly familiar part of the growing season.

But in Gredos, the losses feel particularly cruel because so much of what burns cannot simply be replanted.

Old Vines Up in Smoke

West of Madrid, Garnacha clings to granite and schist slopes at elevation, often in tiny parcels of old bush vines planted 70, 80, sometimes more than 100 years ago. Over the past two decades, those vineyards have attracted a new generation of winemakers drawn by their remarkable transparency and sense of place.

Fernando García of Comando G sees Gredos as far more than a wine region. “Gredos is a spectacular region: a mountainous landscape with wild nature,” he says, “and a long agricultural tradition of vineyards, olive groves, and fruit trees. It is an oasis in the middle of the Iberian Peninsula.”

Pete Irvine of PJ Antipoda points to the vines’ deep, established root systems as something that would require decades to recreate.

“The surrounding forest and vegetation like the holm oaks, chestnuts, wild lavender, and juniper give a unique element to the terroir here,” he says. “When those disappear, their recovery also takes decades.”

That is what makes the fires that swept through Gredos in July different from an ordinary bad vintage. The blaze beginning near Burgohondo on July 22 became part of a massive fire complex across Ávila, Madrid, and Toledo that burned tens of thousands of hectares and forced widespread evacuations.

Daniel Ramos, who has made wine in the area since 1999, estimates that 80% of his crop was lost either directly to fire or potentially to smoke. His winery, fortunately, sits inside the town and survived.

At Indiano Winery, Charles Gotchac watched the flames come within roughly 200 meters of the cellar. Friends, neighbors, and firefighters helped defend the property. Some of his vineyards burned; others spent days beneath smoke. “It was a fucking monster,” he recalls.

That smoke now hangs over the coming vintage metaphorically as much as it did physically.

Gotchac expects to confront smoke taint for the first time. Irvine, whose vineyards escaped the flames but not days of lingering smoke, believes that at low levels it could become “a signature of the vintage,” rather than automatically a defect. Campana is less concerned, noting that grapes were still green during the fires and recalling similarly smoky conditions in 2021 that produced no detectable taint.

Yet the longer you speak with Gredos winemakers, the less they talk about smoke taint and the more they talk about the land itself.

The fires that swept through Spain’s Sierra de Gredos exposed not only the vulnerability of one of Europe’s most exciting wine regions, but also a growing consensus among its winemakers that preserving old vines will require rethinking how the entire landscape is managed.

Neglected Land Adding Fuel to the Fire 

Campana remembers a countryside with more people working it, where farmers and shepherds helped maintain the forests. “When you don’t have people living there taking care of stuff, these things are going to happen,” he says. 

Gotchac agrees, arguing that climate change has made fires more intense, but that neglected landscapes often determine how easily they spread.

García takes that idea a step further. “Large wildfires are the result of a combination of human activity and landscapes with huge amounts of unmanaged vegetation,” he says. “All of this is being amplified by climate change: heatwaves, extremely low relative humidity, and strong winds create ideal conditions for fires to develop into massive, uncontrollable blazes.”

Irvine sees the consequences on the ground. Elderly growers become unable to work their vines. Their children have moved to cities. Another historic vineyard is abandoned, vegetation takes over, and a potential firebreak becomes combustible ground.

“Well-managed, tidy ecological vineyards are fire breaks,” he says. “It would be great if that could be more appreciated and country life be more incentivized.”

Ramos is more combative. “If you don’t control a forest, one day or another, it will be so full of rubbish that it will burn in five minutes without any way to control it,” he says.

Ramos, who remembers harvesting Garnacha in mid-September in 1999 and now regularly starts around August 20 to 24, hardly denies that the climate has changed. But like several growers here, he believes hotter, drier conditions have collided with the disappearance of traditional land stewardship.

His immediate concern is not merely his own crop. It is helping elderly growers access subsidies and keep farming.

“If their vineyard keeps alive,” he says, “we will still have some future.”

Lane says producers are now discussing vineyard recovery, fire prevention, and what they should demand from the government. Ramos believes the catastrophe has finally pushed fiercely independent growers toward working together, while Irvine hopes it leads to greater collaboration on farming practices that make the landscape more resilient.

García believes recovery should begin with what the fires spared. “Gredos deserves to be made green,” he says. “Despite the fire, several villages were left untouched, creating green islands that must become the starting point for regeneration.”

When Stubbornness Means Survival

Gredos has never been an easy country. Its vineyards are small, steep, and scattered, surviving largely because generations of stubborn growers believed difficulty was not the same as futility.

And despite everything that burned, none of the growers interviewed for this story spoke of leaving.

Irvine still talks about altitude, granite, old Garnacha and the strange delicacy these brutal mountains can produce.

“Gredos is just getting started,” he says.

Ramos puts it another way. When things become bleak, he says, sometimes you open one of the region’s wines and remember why you stayed in the first place.

“You realize that this can’t disappear.”

title: 8 Dreamy Home Wine Cellars You’ll Wish Were Yours
summary:
Jaw-dropping wine cellars aren’t just for restaurants. These home cellars prove it.

The post 8 Dreamy Home Wine Cellars You’ll Wish Were Yours appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Long gone are the days of musty, no-frills wine cellars. Creating the proper environment for aging and storage, of course, remains the priority for these utilitarian spaces. But a lot of time and money can go into cultivating a wine collection, so many design-savvy oenophiles opt to show off their treasures in stylish layouts. Whether it weaves in striking lighting, vintage finds, or made-to-order furniture, the contemporary wine cellar is now regarded as yet another room to gather and celebrate. Here are eight eye-catching examples.

An Intimate Tasting Space with Polish

Hillsborough, California

Only four leather chairs surround the marble tasting table anchoring the wine cellar Heather Hilliard brought to life for a private California residence. She wanted to create an intimate, comfortable space for the clients to enjoy wine tastings with a small group of guests, but with “the polished atmosphere and sense of experience you might find in a favorite restaurant,” explains the San Francisco-based designer. It’s joined by stone flooring that grounds the cellar and glass walls that ensure it’s visually open. “The cellar accommodates approximately 1,000 bottles stored horizontally on lit shelves so the collection becomes part of the architecture while remaining easy to view and access,” adds Hilliard.

A Cinematic Cellar Starring Prized Bottles

Greenwich, Connecticut

Since her clients are avid wine collectors, Taylor Lagerloef, founder and principal designer of Studio Lagerloef in New York, designed a cinematic cellar in a Greenwich, Connecticut, home—in collaboration with Cardello Architects and builder Hobbs, Inc.—to showcase an impressive stash. “They didn’t want the collection hidden away; they wanted to live with it,” Lagerloef points out. Along one wall, Lagerloef and her team built open shelving to highlight large-format bottles, favorite labels, and wine crates, and the backlit stone wall further amplifies the display. “The lighting turns rows of bottles into something that feels almost sculptural, and because the room is glass-enclosed and visible from the living space, the collection becomes part of the home’s everyday narrative,” she says. Polished concrete flooring and VeroMetal soffits add intriguing contrast to the wood-paneled ceiling and framed vintage wine map.

A Clandestine Mountainside Cave

Teton Village, Wyoming

Underneath a nearly 10,000-square-foot ski-in/ski-out, stone-and-timber house in Teton Village, Wyoming, CLB Architects dug a well below the lowest footings. Here, the wine cellar, part of an addition, is a departure from the existing dwelling’s traditional mountain architecture. A blackened steel handrail leads down to a massive area capable of holding 7,500 bottles. “The vision was to create a wine cellar that felt like a secret cave carved from solid stone,” says Montana-based CLB Architects principal Sam Ankeny. To enhance the carved effect on the walls, a split-face, natural cleft is mixed with honed Valser Quartz, while the ceiling is lined with subtle barrel-vaulted mahogany on the ceiling to add “warmth and evoke the sensation of being inside a wine barrel,” Ankeny adds. One exterior wall of the chic, subterranean grotto is outfitted with a thin-profile sliding glass system to capture natural light and seamlessly connect to the Rocky Mountain landscape.

A Resort-Like Wine Escape in the Hills

Beverly Hills, California

Boutique hotels were the inspiration for this narrow, four-story abode set high atop a ridge in Beverly Hills. “Solving the long, skinny site problem created an opportunity for many levels and spaces,” says Marc Whipple, founder of Whipple Russell Architects. This includes an entertainment hub including a poker room, theater, and a hybrid wine cellar and custom humidor that the Sherman Oaks-based architecture firm hatched in partnership with Troy Adams Design. Floor-to-ceiling dark-tinted glass reveals illuminated bottle storage that meshes with bespoke furniture, a marble wet bar, Spanish cedar, and Henge lighting. Fresh air and gorgeous views await right outside on the adjacent covered terrace, complete with a cozy fire feature that’s a prime spot to enjoy a glass on a chilly evening.

A Euro-Inspired Shrine to Red Wine

Kleinburg, Ontario

Jessica Neilas, founder and creative director of Toronto-based Wolfe Interior Design, envisioned this cellar in an Ontario home as a place to settle in around the table in the center. ”Somewhere that could accommodate both a quiet glass of wine and a night of revelry,” as she puts it. The client’s passion for red wine translated to deep red marble and burgundy leather paired with aged brass tones. But the most dramatic element is the arched wood-and-glass enclosure. “There is a deliberate transition from the brighter architecture outside into something darker, warmer, and more intimate,” says Neilas. “It feels almost like looking into a tiny European bar or enoteca—a little hidden room where you expect to find great wine, music, conversation, and people lingering much longer than they intended.”

Climate-Controlled Centerpiece with a Luxe Touch

Atlanta, Georgia

The terrace level of an Atlanta townhouse beckons with a spa and golf simulator, but the bar, flanked by a duo of climate-controlled wine and spirits cellars is the focal point. Local designer Robert Brown, in collaboration with Kingdom Millworks for construction and cabinet designer Studio Entourage, opted for a dark grasscloth wallcovering paired with high-gloss trim, custom millwork, and steel doors.”Brass and marble accents add a luxurious touch, while warm-stained oak racking and limestone flooring bring warmth and balance to the space,” explains Brown. “The combination of textures, materials, and contrasting finishes creates a sophisticated backdrop that allows the artwork to take center stage.”

A Solar-Powered Hangout Spot

Chicago, Illinois

When local architect Matt Nardella, co-founder of Moss Design, revamped his Chicago basement, he craved a transparent, glass-fronted cellar that invited everyday hangouts. “This isn’t a space I just run down to in order to grab a bottle,” he says. “The cellar has become the place where we listen to music, entertain friends, and let the evening unfold.” Moss’s choice of materials—walnut, steel, polished concrete, and travertine—in the solar-powered cellar are intentionally beautiful in their raw state, and carry evidence of their roots, much like wine. The same two slabs of travertine were used to craft a countertop, backsplash, and custom tasting table, “allowing the material to move elegantly from architecture to furniture,” adds Nardella. 

A Nostalgic Study for World-Class Wine

Highland Park, Texas

Following the remodel of a Highland Park house, the first thing one notices when heading downstairs is the cellar. It’s en route to the cinema beyond, so Naina Hotchkiss and Allison McAfee, partners and principal designers of Dallas-based Park Interiors, wanted it to feel like a transition into something relaxed, “somewhere that slows you down rather than a space you simply pass through. We leaned into a moody, confident palette and treated it almost like a study or trophy room that happened to house exceptional wine,” explains Hotchkiss. Velvety green plaster walls play with bespoke, brass-accented white oak cabinetry, and an antique Persian rug and framed tennis rackets infuse the space with an air of nostalgia. “The way every object was chosen and placed, down to the smallest detail tells you everything about who lives here, their passions, their wins, and their sense of humor about displaying it all so unapologetically,” says McAfee.
